chapters.title: PESTLE & the External Business Environment
chapters.description: How firms analyse macro-environmental change and translate it into business effects.

questions.stem: What does PESTLE primarily help a business analyse?

options.text: Its internal employee performance
Its external macro-environment
Only its direct competitors
Only its financial statements

questions.explanation: PESTLE scans broad external forces that can create opportunities, threats and strategic pressures.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Which expansion of PESTLE is correct?

options.text: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental
Pricing, Employment, Sales, Trade, Logistics, Efficiency
Political, Ethical, Strategic, Technical, Labour, External
Planning, Economic, Social, Tax, Leadership, Ecology

questions.explanation: The six categories are Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Which is the best distinction between a political and a legal factor?

options.text: Political factors concern government direction; legal factors concern binding rules and compliance.
Political factors are internal; legal factors are external.
Political factors affect costs; legal factors affect only demand.
There is no useful distinction.

questions.explanation: Political analysis considers policy direction and stability, while legal analysis concerns enforceable requirements such as employment or competition law.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Which response shows the strongest PESTLE analysis?

options.text: List AI under Technology and stop.
Explain how AI changes costs or demand, classify the opportunity or threat, and propose a response.
Describe only the firm’s current software.
Assume every technological change benefits every firm.

questions.explanation: Good PESTLE work connects an external change to a business mechanism, impact and strategic response.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: A manufacturer faces carbon reporting rules and customers seeking lower-impact products. Which PESTLE reading is best?

options.text: Only a legal threat
Only an environmental opportunity
Both compliance pressure and a possible market opportunity
An internal staffing issue only

questions.explanation: The same development can create compliance costs while opening demand for sustainable products.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What is a limitation of PESTLE?

options.text: It can become outdated and subjective if not prioritised and refreshed.
It guarantees accurate forecasts.
It fully measures internal capabilities.
It removes uncertainty from decisions.

questions.explanation: PESTLE is a broad scan, not a prediction machine; it can age quickly and encourage analysis paralysis.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why should managers prioritise PESTLE factors rather than treat every item equally?

options.text: All factors have identical effects.
Priority helps focus monitoring and action on the most material uncertainties.
Only legal factors can affect strategy.
Prioritisation converts external factors into internal resources.

questions.explanation: Ranking factors by likely impact and uncertainty makes the analysis useful for decisions.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: A central bank raises interest rates. Which business effect is most direct?

options.text: Borrowing and investment become more expensive.
Employment law changes automatically.
The population becomes younger.
Carbon emissions immediately fall.

questions.explanation: Interest rates affect financing costs, investment and interest-sensitive demand.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes and linked PESTLE materials

questions.stem: Which factor is technological rather than merely social?

options.text: The population is ageing.
A government changes VAT.
A new automation process reduces unit production cost.
Consumers prefer locally made goods.

questions.explanation: Process innovation belongs to Technology; preferences and demographics are Social.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes and linked PESTLE materials

questions.stem: Why should a PESTLE analysis define the market and decision first?

options.text: Every industry faces identical risks.
It converts external factors into internal strengths.
It prevents future change.
The same external change can have different effects across firms and decisions.

questions.explanation: Scope is needed before an external fact can be translated into a relevant business impact.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes and linked PESTLE materials

questions.stem: A new minimum-wage law is best classified how?

options.text: Social only, because workers are people.
Legal, with possible cost and productivity effects.
Environmental, because wages affect resources.
Technological, because payroll is digital.

questions.explanation: The binding rule is Legal, though its consequences can affect costs, hiring and operations.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes and linked PESTLE materials

questions.stem: What is the best way to keep PESTLE useful over time?

options.text: List every possible fact without ranking.
Use it instead of internal analysis.
Treat it as a monitored, periodically refreshed set of priorities.
Complete it once and never revisit it.

questions.explanation: External conditions change, so assumptions and priorities need review.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 1 notes and linked PESTLE materials

questions.stem: A general election creates uncertainty about future tax policy before any law changes. Which category is most direct?

options.text: Environmental
Political
Legal
Technological

questions.explanation: The uncertainty comes from political decision-making; a legal factor would be an enacted rule or regulation.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What does real income measure?

options.text: Income adjusted for changes in the price level
Income before tax only
The amount held in cash
Revenue earned by a firm

questions.explanation: Real income captures purchasing power by accounting for inflation.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Which example is a process innovation?

options.text: Using automation to manufacture the same product more efficiently
Launching a product with a new feature
Changing the legal name of a firm
Hiring more sales staff

questions.explanation: Process innovation changes how a good or service is produced rather than the product itself.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: A rise in ransomware attacks is most directly relevant to which PESTLE dimension?

options.text: Technological
Social
Environmental
Political

questions.explanation: Cybersecurity risk is tied most directly to digital technology, although it can also create legal and reputational consequences.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a physical environmental risk?

options.text: Flooding disrupts a supplier’s factory
A new carbon-reporting law takes effect
Interest rates rise
Consumer tastes shift towards subscriptions

questions.explanation: Flooding is a physical climate or environmental event; reporting rules are primarily legal.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Which pair is most useful when prioritising PESTLE issues?

options.text: Likely impact and likelihood
Alphabetical order and report length
Number of departments and office size
Past profit and share price only

questions.explanation: Managers should focus monitoring and action on changes that are both plausible and materially important.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Why can the same external change be both an opportunity and a threat?

options.text: External changes affect only new firms
Its effect depends on the firm’s capabilities, position and response
PESTLE categories are always mutually contradictory
Every law benefits all firms equally

questions.explanation: A change can favour firms prepared to adapt while harming competitors that cannot respond effectively.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Which sequence turns a PESTLE observation into useful analysis?

options.text: Choose a response, ignore evidence, then assign a category
List categories, calculate accounting profit, then stop
Predict an exact future and avoid updating it
Identify evidence, explain the mechanism, assess impact, then choose a response

questions.explanation: Strong analysis connects evidence to a causal business impact and an appropriate action.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: A government announces a sustained programme of higher public spending and also signals that it will maintain strict control of public finances. Which PESTLE category is most directly concerned with these developments?

options.text: Legal
Economic
Environmental
Political

questions.explanation: Government spending and fiscal policy are classified as Political in this PESTLE teaching framework; they also have economic effects.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 1

questions.stem: An SME completes a PESTLE analysis and concludes that it has a strong internal capability to exploit a new market. Why should this conclusion not be treated as a PESTLE finding by itself?

options.text: PESTLE focuses on the external environment and does not assess internal strengths, weaknesses or capabilities
PESTLE is designed only to analyse financial statements
PESTLE only considers environmental issues
PESTLE cannot be used for strategic planning

questions.explanation: PESTLE examines external conditions. Internal capabilities belong in an internal analysis such as SWOT.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 2

questions.stem: A bakery’s customers have experienced rising prices for many goods. The bakery is concerned that, even where nominal household incomes rise, customers may have less purchasing power. Which PESTLE factor is most relevant?

options.text: Political stability
Real incomes and purchasing power
Competition law
Access to raw materials

questions.explanation: Real income measures purchasing power after allowing for changes in prices.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 3

questions.stem: An Irish business is considering selling more products in the UK. The euro falls in value relative to sterling. What is the most direct effect of this currency depreciation on goods imported from the UK into Ireland?

options.text: There is necessarily no effect
Imports become dearer
Imports become cheaper
Exports necessarily become dearer

questions.explanation: A weaker euro buys fewer pounds, raising the euro cost of UK imports, other things equal.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 4

questions.stem: An SME bakery finds that changes in the age structure of the population are altering demand for different types of baked goods. Which PESTLE category does this illustrate?

options.text: Technological
Legal
Social
Political

questions.explanation: Age structure and demographics are Social factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 5

questions.stem: A bakery introduces automated production equipment and robotics to speed up its production process and reduce costs. Which PESTLE category best captures this development?

options.text: Technological
Political
Environmental
Social

questions.explanation: Automation and robotics fall under Technological factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 6

questions.stem: A company must change how it stores and processes customers’ personal information because of the GDPR. Which PESTLE category should this issue be placed under?

options.text: Legal
Economic
Social
Political

questions.explanation: Data-protection obligations are Legal factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 7

questions.stem: A business is assessing how climate change, carbon-reduction pressures and the transition to lower-emission operations could affect its costs and long-term plans. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant?

options.text: Environmental
Technological
Legal
Social

questions.explanation: Climate and sustainability pressures are Environmental factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 8

questions.stem: A manager uses PESTLE analysis to identify an emerging external threat before it has a serious effect on the business. Which advantage of PESTLE is being demonstrated?

options.text: Early risk identification
Elimination of uncertainty
Objective measurement of all factors
Assessment of internal strengths

questions.explanation: PESTLE can identify external risks early.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 9

questions.stem: An Irish SME bakery is considering expanding into the UK. The management team is particularly concerned that changes in the euro–sterling exchange rate could alter the cost of ingredients and other imported inputs. Which PESTLE factor should it examine most directly?

options.text: Economic
Technological
Social
Legal

questions.explanation: Exchange-rate movements are Economic factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 11

questions.stem: An SME wants to improve its green credentials and asks managers to use PESTLE analysis. The team produces a long list of climate, carbon-pricing and sustainability issues but cannot decide which ones should influence its strategy. Which disadvantage of PESTLE is most clearly illustrated?

options.text: High implementation cost
Objective measurement of all factors
Ignoring internal factors
Risk of analysis paralysis

questions.explanation: An unprioritised list prevents decisions: analysis paralysis.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 12

questions.stem: An Irish bakery is researching whether demand in the UK may differ from demand in Ireland because of differences in customer tastes, culture and demographic patterns. Which PESTLE category is most relevant?

options.text: Social
Legal
Political
Environmental

questions.explanation: Culture, preferences and demographics are Social factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 13

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company is considering moving some operations from Cork to Poland. Before making the investment, managers want to assess how regulation and employment-law requirements, including statutory minimum-wage rules, could affect the operation. Which PESTLE category is this?

options.text: Economic
Technological
Social
Legal

questions.explanation: Regulation, employment law and statutory wage requirements are Legal factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 14

questions.stem: An IT company is considering a major new investment in Ireland. Its managers want to understand how rapid developments in AI, digitalisation, payment systems and cybersecurity could affect the competitiveness of the investment. Which PESTLE category should they focus on?

options.text: Political
Social
Environmental
Technological

questions.explanation: AI, digitalisation and cybersecurity are Technological factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 16

questions.stem: An indigenous small IT company is considering expanding its product range. The owners believe that technological innovation could allow it to develop new products and increase the added value offered to customers. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant to this external opportunity?

options.text: Legal
Political
Environmental
Technological

questions.explanation: Technological innovation can create external product-development opportunities.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 18

questions.stem: An SME agri-business is considering moving manufacturing to China. Its board wants to assess the possible impact of tariffs, trade policy and geopolitical risk on the proposed move. Which PESTLE category should be used?

options.text: Technological
Political
Environmental
Social

questions.explanation: Tariffs, trade policy and geopolitical risk are Political factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 19

questions.stem: An agri-business is also considering how access to raw materials and longer-term sustainability issues could affect the proposed manufacturing strategy. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant?

options.text: Political
Legal
Environmental
Social

questions.explanation: Natural-resource availability and sustainability are Environmental factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 20

questions.stem: A Cork medical-device exporter faces a new EU product-certification rule and a simultaneous fall in sterling. Which analysis best separates the two developments?

options.text: Certification is a legal factor; sterling depreciation is an economic factor that may reduce euro receipts from UK sales.
Certification is technological; sterling depreciation necessarily increases euro receipts.
Certification is social; exchange-rate changes cannot affect competitiveness.
Both are political factors, because governments influence each.

questions.explanation: Product-certification requirements are legal constraints. A weaker pound can reduce the euro value of unchanged sterling receipts, so the exchange-rate change is economic.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q1; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Shareholder Wealth, Present Value & Profit
chapters.description: Time value of money, shareholder wealth, present value, NPV and profit concepts.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines shareholder wealth?

options.text: The firm's total accounting profit in the current year
The present value of expected future cash returns to equity owners
The total value of the firm's outstanding bonds
The value of the firm's physical assets before liabilities

questions.explanation: Shareholder wealth concerns the value of expected future returns to equity owners.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 21

questions.stem: Why is €100 received today generally worth more than €100 received in one year?

options.text: Today’s money can be invested and future payment involves delay and risk.
Future money is legally invalid.
Inflation is always exactly equal to interest.
Money received today has no opportunity cost.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost, time preference and risk make earlier cash more valuable.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Which formula correctly calculates the present value of a single future sum?

options.text: PV=FV(1+r)^n
PV = FV / (1 + r)^n
PV=FV-rn
PV = FV / (r + n)

questions.explanation: Divide the future sum by its compound discount factor.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 25

questions.stem: Holding the future cash flow and time period constant, what happens when the discount rate rises?

options.text: Present value rises
Present value falls
Present value remains unchanged
Present value becomes equal to future value

questions.explanation: A larger discount denominator lowers present value for an unchanged positive cash flow.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 27

questions.stem: A project costs €1,000 now and has a present value of future cash inflows of €1,150. What is its NPV?
questions.explanation: NPV equals present value of inflows minus the initial cost: €1,150−€1,000=€150.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Under the standard NPV rule, which project should normally be accepted?

options.text: A project with NPV below zero
A project with NPV above zero
Only a project with no future cash flows
Any project regardless of NPV

questions.explanation: A positive NPV adds value at the required return.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: At a 10% discount rate, what is the present value of €5 received in one year, rounded to two decimals?
questions.explanation: €5/1.10 equals approximately €4.55.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Which expression gives accounting-style profit in the basic model?

options.text: TR+TC
TR−TC
TC−TR
P−Q

questions.explanation: Profit is total revenue minus total cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: A firm reports a positive accounting profit, but the return is below what the owner could earn from the next-best alternative. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Economic profit must be positive
The project necessarily maximises shareholder wealth
Economic profit may be negative because opportunity cost is not covered
Opportunity cost is irrelevant once accounting profit is positive

questions.explanation: Implicit opportunity costs can exceed the positive accounting profit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 33

questions.stem: What is the future value of €100 invested for one year at 5%?
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes and NPV assessment material

questions.stem: A €121 payment is due in two years and the discount rate is 10%. What is its present value?
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes and NPV assessment material

questions.stem: Why should cash flows at different dates not simply be added?

options.text: They must first be converted to values at a common date.
Future cash is always worthless.
Only costs can be discounted.
Time has no effect on value.

questions.explanation: Discounting makes dated amounts economically comparable.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes and NPV assessment material

questions.stem: A project has NPV equal to zero at the required return. What does that imply?

options.text: It must be rejected as a loss.
Its accounting profit is zero in every year.
It earns exactly the required return and neither adds nor destroys value.
It produces no revenue.

questions.explanation: Zero NPV means discounted inflows exactly cover the investment at the opportunity cost of capital.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes and NPV assessment material

questions.stem: Which change can raise shareholder value even if current accounting profit falls?

options.text: An investment that creates sufficiently large discounted future cash flows.
A project with a negative NPV.
Ignoring risk in every forecast.
Paying any cost solely to raise sales.

questions.explanation: Wealth maximisation considers the timing and risk of future returns, not one period alone.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 notes and NPV assessment material

questions.stem: Two equally certain €100 payments are due in one year and two years. At a positive discount rate, which has the higher present value?

options.text: Neither has a present value
The payment due in one year
The payment due in two years
They have equal present values

questions.explanation: The earlier payment is discounted for less time, so its present value is higher.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Which formula gives the future value of principal P compounded m times per year for t years at annual rate r?

options.text: P+rmt

questions.explanation: Compounding m times per year applies the periodic rate r/m over mt periods.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: How is greater risk commonly reflected in a present-value calculation?

options.text: By ignoring the timing of cash flows
By adding risk directly to every cash flow
By setting the project cost to zero
By using a higher required discount rate

questions.explanation: A higher required return discounts risky future cash flows more heavily.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Which is an implicit cost when calculating economic profit?

options.text: Income the owner forgoes by using their own time in the business
Wages paid to an employee
Rent paid under a lease
An electricity bill

questions.explanation: Implicit costs are opportunity costs of owner-supplied resources without an explicit cash payment.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What is the normal return to an entrepreneur?

options.text: A legally guaranteed dividend
The minimum opportunity-cost return needed to keep resources in the business
Any accounting loss
Total sales revenue

questions.explanation: Normal return is part of economic cost because it is the return forgone from the next-best use.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What does zero economic profit normally mean?

options.text: The firm covers explicit costs and all opportunity costs, including a normal return
The firm has no revenue
The firm has zero accounting profit in every case
The firm must immediately close

questions.explanation: Zero economic profit means resources earn exactly their opportunity cost, not that the business earns nothing in accounting terms.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Why does accepting a positive-NPV project tend to increase shareholder wealth?

options.text: Accounting rules remove all risk
Future cash flows are not discounted
The present value of expected benefits exceeds the current cost
The project guarantees the largest possible revenue

questions.explanation: Positive NPV represents value created above the required return.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: An owner invests €50,000 of personal funds that could earn 4% elsewhere. What is the annual opportunity cost of that capital?
questions.explanation: Four per cent of €50,000 is €2,000, which is an implicit economic cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: If marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue for the last unit produced, what does the basic marginal rule suggest?

options.text: Increasing output must increase profit
Revenue and cost are irrelevant
The firm is necessarily technically inefficient
Reducing output may increase profit

questions.explanation: When MC exceeds MR, the last unit reduces profit, so output should be reconsidered downward.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 2 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate when calculating the present value of several annual cash flows?

options.text: Add the undiscounted cash flows and discount the total once using Year 1
Discount each cash flow for its own time period and then add the present values
Use the risk-free rate even when a required return is supplied
Round every intermediate step to the nearest whole euro

questions.explanation: Discount each cash flow for the time until it is received, then sum.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 29

questions.stem: Why is shareholder wealth maximisation broader than simple profit maximisation?

options.text: It ignores risk but includes tax
It focuses only on the largest annual profit
It accounts for the timing and risk of expected future returns
It treats all stakeholders as equity owners

questions.explanation: Timing and risk matter as well as the amount of returns.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 22

questions.stem: Which is not itself a reason to discount future money?

options.text: Opportunity cost
Time preference
Risk premium
Market share

questions.explanation: Market share is not itself a reason to discount money.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 23

questions.stem: An investor requires a higher return from an oil-exploration project than from a safe deposit. Which concept best explains the difference?

options.text: Fixed cost
Risk premium
Accounting depreciation
Consumer surplus

questions.explanation: Additional investment risk can require a risk premium.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 24

questions.stem: What is the approximate present value of €110 received in one year when the discount rate is 10%?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 26

questions.stem: A share has expected returns of €5, €6 and €7 at the ends of Years 1, 2 and 3. At a 10% discount rate, what is their approximate total present value?
questions.explanation: €5/1.10 = €4.545455; €6/1.10² = €4.958678; €7/1.10³ = €5.259204. Add before rounding: €14.763336 ≈ €14.76. The earlier €14.77 used rounded intermediate values.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 28

questions.stem: A project has an NPV of −€4,500. What decision follows from the standard NPV rule?

options.text: Accept because all cash inflows are positive
Accept because the initial investment is already paid
Remain indifferent
Reject because the project destroys value relative to the required return

questions.explanation: Negative NPV fails the required return, so reject under the standard rule.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 31

questions.stem: Let VC denote variable cost per unit and FC total fixed cost. Which set of identities is correct?

options.text: π=TR+TC; TR=P-Q; TC=VC-FC
π=TR-TC; TR=P× Q; TC=VC× Q+FC
π=TC-TR; TR=P× VC; TC=Q+FC
π=P+Q; TR=VC× Q; TC=P× Q

questions.explanation: Profit = revenue − cost; revenue = price × quantity; total cost = unit variable cost × quantity + fixed cost. Here VC means variable cost per unit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 32

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes real and nominal required rates of return?

options.text: Real required returns are determined by inflation alone
A real required return reflects opportunity cost, time preference and risk; a nominal required return also allows for expected inflation
Nominal required returns must equal the risk-free rate
Real required returns automatically fall as investment risk rises

questions.explanation: A real required return reflects opportunity cost, time preference and risk. A nominal required return also allows for expected inflation; cash flows and rates must use consistent nominal or real terms.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 34

questions.stem: Which management decision would most directly increase shareholder value, all else equal?

options.text: Increasing expected costs without changing revenue
Delaying the same cash flow while keeping risk unchanged
Increasing expected future cash returns without increasing the required return
Raising the discount rate applied to unchanged cash flows

questions.explanation: Larger expected returns at the same required return increase present value.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 35

questions.stem: A firm expects profits per share of €4, €5 and €6 in Years 1–3. Investors require a return of 10%. What is the present value of one share?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 36

questions.stem: A company expects profits per share of €8, €9 and €10 in Years 1–3. The required return is 8%. What is the present value of one share?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 37

questions.stem: Holding expected future profits constant, what is the effect of an increase in investors’ required rate of return on the current value of a share?

options.text: It increases the share value
It first increases and then reduces the share value
It has no effect
It reduces the share value

questions.explanation: A higher required return lowers the present value of unchanged positive future profits.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 38

questions.stem: A firm sells 2,000 units at €25 per unit. What is total revenue?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 39

questions.stem: A firm’s total revenue is €120,000 and it sells 4,000 units. What is the price per unit?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 40

questions.stem: A firm produces 5,000 units, has a variable cost of €12 per unit and fixed costs of €20,000. What is total cost?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 41

questions.stem: A firm sells 10,000 units at €30 each. Variable cost is €18 per unit and fixed costs are €60,000. What is profit?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 42

questions.stem: A firm sells at €40 per unit, has a variable cost of €25 per unit and fixed costs of €50,000. What is profit at an output of 6,000 units?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 43

questions.stem: A firm’s price is €50, variable cost is €30 per unit and fixed costs are €100,000. What output gives zero profit?

options.text: 2,000 units
5,000 units
6,667 units
3,333 units

questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 44

questions.stem: An investment pays €550 at the end of Year 1 and €726 at the end of Year 2, with no other payments. At a 10% annual discount rate, what is the combined present value?
questions.explanation: Discount each payment for its own time period: €550/1.10 + €726/1.10² = €500 + €600 = €1,100. Discounting the total for just one period misstates timing.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #2 — PV, FV, NPV and profit; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c815ca6b4f223c97d97c8

questions.stem: A project costs €1,000 today and pays €660 at the end of each of Years 1 and 2. There are no other cash flows. At a 10% required return, what are its NPV and the standard investment decision?

options.text: €320; accept
−€145.45; reject
€200; accept
€145.45; accept

questions.explanation: NPV = −€1,000 + €660/1.10 + €660/1.10² = €145.45 after rounding. The positive NPV supports acceptance under the standard rule.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #2 — PV, FV, NPV and profit; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c815ca6b4f223c97d97c8

questions.stem: You invest €800 for three years at 5% interest compounded annually, with no withdrawals. What is the future value, rounded to cents?
questions.explanation: FV = €800 × 1.05³ = €926.10. €920 uses simple interest rather than annual compounding.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #2 — PV, FV, NPV and profit; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c815ca6b4f223c97d97c8

questions.stem: A firm charges €35 per unit, incurs €21 variable cost per unit and has €42,000 fixed costs. Assuming every unit produced is sold, what output gives zero profit?

options.text: 1,200 units
2,000 units
3,000 units
5,000 units

questions.explanation: Contribution per unit is €35 − €21 = €14. Break-even output is €42,000/€14 = 3,000 units.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #2 — PV, FV, NPV and profit; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c815ca6b4f223c97d97c8

questions.stem: An Irish SME pays €100,000 today for a machine generating €60,000 at the end of each of the next two years, with no scrap value. At a 10% discount rate, which conclusion is closest?

options.text: NPV is approximately −€4,132; reject.
NPV is approximately +€9,091, because only year two is discounted.
NPV is +€20,000, because discounting is irrelevant over two years.
NPV is approximately +€4,132; accept if risk and other assumptions are adequately reflected.

questions.explanation: NPV = −100,000 + 60,000/1.10 + 60,000/(1.10²) = +€4,132.23. A positive NPV supports acceptance when the discount rate and cash-flow assumptions adequately reflect risk.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q2; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Markets, Economic Systems & Price Signals
chapters.description: Market coordination, economic systems, efficiency and dispersed information.

questions.stem: What is a market in the economic sense?

options.text: Only a physical shop
An arrangement through which buyers and sellers interact and exchange
A government department that sets every price
A firm’s internal accounting system

questions.explanation: A market coordinates exchange between buyers and sellers; it need not be a physical place.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: Which system relies mainly on decentralised prices and private decisions to allocate resources?

options.text: Command economy
Market economy
Subsistence accounting
Central budget system

questions.explanation: Market economies coordinate activity largely through voluntary exchange and price signals.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: Which system relies mainly on central authorities setting output and allocation decisions?

options.text: Command economy
Competitive market economy
Informal resale market
Mixed pricing system

questions.explanation: In a command system, central planning replaces much decentralised market coordination.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: Why are modern economies commonly described as mixed?

options.text: They contain no markets.
They combine market allocation with government provision, regulation and intervention.
They prohibit private ownership.
They use only barter.

questions.explanation: Most economies blend market coordination with public rules and services.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: What does a rising market price usually signal to producers, other things equal?

options.text: The good has become less scarce relative to demand.
There may be an incentive to supply more.
Consumers have stopped valuing the good.
Production must legally cease.

questions.explanation: A higher price can communicate scarcity and reward producers for expanding supply.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: What is the “invisible hand” idea used to illustrate?

options.text: Central planners know every local detail.
Self-interested exchange can coordinate activity through market signals.
Every market outcome is fair.
Prices contain no information.

questions.explanation: The concept describes decentralised coordination emerging from individual decisions.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: What is Hayek’s dispersed-knowledge argument?

options.text: All useful knowledge is held by one regulator.
Relevant knowledge is spread across individuals, and prices help communicate it.
Knowledge has no role in allocation.
Firms never respond to local information.

questions.explanation: Prices can condense and transmit information that no single planner fully possesses.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: What does technical efficiency mean?

options.text: Producing the maximum output from given inputs, or using the fewest inputs for an output
Ensuring everyone receives the same income
Setting price above equilibrium
Maximising the number of regulations

questions.explanation: Technical efficiency concerns avoiding waste in the production process.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What does Pareto efficiency mean?

options.text: Everyone has equal wealth.
No one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
Government spending is zero.
Every producer earns identical profit.

questions.explanation: Pareto efficiency is about possible mutually beneficial reallocation, not equality.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why does economic efficiency not automatically imply equity?

options.text: Efficiency measures distributional fairness directly.
An efficient allocation can still distribute benefits very unequally.
Equity and efficiency are identical concepts.
Equity applies only to production technology.

questions.explanation: Efficiency concerns waste and gains from trade; equity concerns fairness of distribution.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What does I, Pencil mainly illustrate?

options.text: A pencil is made by one self-sufficient worker.
Prices eliminate every inequality.
Central plans never use information.
Complex production can be coordinated through dispersed knowledge without one person directing the whole process.

questions.explanation: The example shows many specialised contributors coordinated by exchange and price signals.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes and I, Pencil

questions.stem: Why can a shortage communicate useful information?

options.text: It indicates that at the current price desired purchases exceed planned sales.
It proves demand has disappeared.
It means the price is above equilibrium.
It guarantees fair allocation.

questions.explanation: Excess demand signals relative scarcity and creates pressure for adjustment.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes and I, Pencil

questions.stem: Why might government intervention coexist with market allocation in a mixed economy?

options.text: Government acts only when demand is vertical.
Markets may coordinate many choices while policy addresses public goods, externalities or distribution.
A mixed economy contains no private firms.
Intervention removes every price.

questions.explanation: Mixed systems combine decentralised exchange with regulation and public provision.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes and I, Pencil

questions.stem: What does a price signal not guarantee?

options.text: That producers may respond to profitability.
That the resulting distribution is fair.
That buyers and sellers receive information about scarcity.
That incentives can change behaviour.

questions.explanation: Prices coordinate incentives but do not by themselves settle equity.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4 notes and I, Pencil

questions.stem: What is the coordinating role of a market price?

options.text: It is set only by producers
It communicates relative scarcity and helps align buyer and seller decisions
It guarantees equal incomes
It removes all uncertainty

questions.explanation: Prices summarise changing conditions and guide decentralised choices.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: When a scarce product’s price rises, how can it ration demand?

options.text: Every buyer purchases more
Supply automatically becomes zero
The product becomes legally prohibited
Some buyers reduce quantity demanded or leave the market

questions.explanation: A higher price discourages lower-valued uses and reduces quantity demanded.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: How does a higher expected selling price generally encourage suppliers?

options.text: It guarantees technical efficiency
It eliminates consumer choice
It increases the reward for bringing resources into that market
It removes production costs

questions.explanation: Potential revenue gives producers an incentive to expand supply where feasible.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What is a Pareto improvement?

options.text: A change that gives everyone equal income
Any technically efficient production plan
A change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off
Any change that raises total revenue

questions.explanation: Pareto improvement is defined by improving someone’s position with no loss to others.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What information challenge does a command economy face?

options.text: A central authority must gather and process widely dispersed, changing information
It cannot issue any production instructions
It has no public sector
Consumers always set output directly

questions.explanation: Central planning can struggle to match the detail and speed of local knowledge.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: An allocation is technically efficient but leaves large income differences. Which distinction matters?

options.text: Any inequality proves more output could be made with the same inputs
Efficiency does not determine equality of distribution
Technical efficiency requires identical incomes
Income differences automatically establish Pareto inefficiency

questions.explanation: Production and allocation efficiency are different questions from distributional equality.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–4, efficiency and equity

questions.stem: Hardware shops charge higher prices for snow shovels after a big snowstorm. What role do prices play in the snow-shovel market?

options.text: In an emergency, prices must remain fixed; therefore, prices do not play a role in this case
Higher prices incentivise distributors to ship more snow shovels into the area to meet the increased demand
Prices signal when price gouging is taking place so authorities can step in to prevent it
In such a natural disaster, prices do not efficiently guide the invisible hand

questions.explanation: Higher prices encourage suppliers to direct additional stock towards increased demand.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 46

questions.stem: In the introductory competitive-market model without relevant market failures, how do price signals support coordination?

options.text: They convey information and align incentives, helping self-interested decisions direct resources towards valued uses
They eliminate the need for firms to respond to consumer preferences
They provide information but cannot influence production incentives
They require a central authority to determine every household purchase

questions.explanation: All three statements describe price signals within the competitive-market framework; this depends on the absence of relevant market failures.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 47

questions.stem: Commuters in Beijing find it difficult to get a cab at rush hour while hundreds of cabs lie idle outside cab companies. Demand and fuel prices have risen, but the government has left the base fare unchanged. What government action is likely to correct the situation?

options.text: Lift the price control on the base fare for cabs
Restrict the entry of new cabs
Regulate the cab market
Reduce income tax on commuters

questions.explanation: Removing the binding fare control allows price to adjust to demand and supply conditions.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 48

questions.stem: How do profits and losses allocate resources in a market economy?

options.text: Profits attract resources and entry to valued products; losses encourage reallocation or exit
Profits prevent new entry while losses require firms to expand
Profits and losses have no influence on investment decisions
Losses attract resources because they demonstrate high unmet profitability

questions.explanation: Profits attract resources and entry; losses encourage reallocation or exit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 49

questions.stem: Which of the following is true of the market economy?

options.text: It generates lower economic output than a command economy
It aligns incentives but fails to coordinate economic agents
It inherently facilitates coordination between economic agents and aligns incentives
It facilitates coordination between economic agents but misaligns incentives

questions.explanation: Prices help coordinate decentralised decisions and align incentives in the market model.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 50

questions.stem: The concept of the invisible hand was introduced by:

options.text: John Keynes
Milton Friedman
Adam Smith
Karl Marx

questions.explanation: Adam Smith introduced the invisible-hand concept.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 51

questions.stem: Which outcome describes the intended benefits of the invisible hand in the introductory competitive-market model?

options.text: Competition can encourage efficient methods, improved products and lower prices
Self-interest guarantees efficient outcomes even with externalities or monopoly power
Competition removes any incentive to improve products
Self-interest ensures every firm earns permanent economic profit

questions.explanation: These are the intended competitive-market benefits in the introductory model, not guarantees for every market.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 52

questions.stem: The concept of the invisible hand refers to:

options.text: A central authority allocating every productive resource
Individuals making decisions in their own self-interest
The Federal Reserve setting interest rates
Government intervention

questions.explanation: Decentralised self-interested decisions can coordinate through prices.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 53

questions.stem: The concept of self-interest, as understood in the invisible-hand model, refers to:

options.text: Profit-maximising behaviour
Rational behaviour
Self-regarding behaviour
Selfish behaviour

questions.explanation: Self-regarding means pursuing one’s own objectives or welfare; it does not require selfishness.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 54

questions.stem: A sudden shortage of cocoa raises its price. A confectionery firm switches to recipes using less cocoa without learning why the shortage arose. Which interpretation most closely reflects Hayek’s argument?

options.text: Only a central authority can coordinate a response to the shortage.
Price signals remove scarcity rather than changing responses to it.
Prices communicate dispersed information and induce economising without every decision-maker knowing the underlying cause.
A higher cocoa price proves that demand must have increased.

questions.explanation: Hayek’s price-system argument is that prices communicate dispersed information. The higher cocoa price encourages economising even when firms do not know the cause of scarcity.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q3; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

questions.stem: A profitable market attracts new independent suppliers over time. Assuming demand and input costs do not change, which sequence is most consistent with competition and Smith’s market coordination?

options.text: Market supply shifts left, price rises, and profits necessarily increase indefinitely.
Individual firms gain permanent pricing power simply because more firms enter.
Market supply shifts right, equilibrium price falls, and above-normal economic profits tend to be competed away.
Demand shifts right, price rises, and entry is discouraged.

questions.explanation: With demand and input costs unchanged, entry increases market supply. Equilibrium price falls and competitive pressure tends to erode above-normal economic profits.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q4; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Demand, Supply & Curve Shifts
chapters.description: Demand and supply behaviour, movements, determinants and functional estimation.

questions.stem: What does quantity demanded mean?

options.text: The amount consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price
The amount firms are legally required to produce
All goods consumers might like for free
The stock currently held by sellers

questions.explanation: Demand requires both willingness and ability to purchase at a specified price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: What does the law of demand state, other things equal?

options.text: Quantity demanded rises when price rises.
Quantity demanded falls when price rises.
Demand never responds to price.
Supply falls when price falls.

questions.explanation: The demand curve slopes downward because higher own-price is associated with lower quantity demanded, ceteris paribus.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: What does the law of supply state, other things equal?

options.text: Quantity supplied tends to rise when price rises.
Quantity supplied always falls when price rises.
Supply is unrelated to price.
Demand rises when production costs rise.

questions.explanation: Higher prices generally make supplying additional units more attractive.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the major factors that shifts the demand curve when it changes?

options.text: The price of the good itself
The price of complementary goods
The price of substitute goods
Income

questions.explanation: A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along its demand curve.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 66

questions.stem: Consumers develop a stronger preference for a product. What is the likely effect?

options.text: Demand shifts right.
A movement up the same demand curve only
Supply shifts left.
Demand shifts left.

questions.explanation: A change in tastes is a non-price determinant that shifts the demand curve.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Income rises for a normal good. What happens to demand, other things equal?

options.text: It shifts left.
It shifts right.
It becomes vertical.
It is unchanged by definition.

questions.explanation: Demand for a normal good increases as consumer income rises.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Tea and coffee are substitutes. If the price of tea falls, what is the likely effect on demand for coffee?

options.text: Coffee demand shifts right.
Coffee demand shifts left.
Coffee supply shifts left.
There is only a movement along coffee supply.

questions.explanation: Cheaper tea draws some buyers away from its substitute, coffee.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Printers and ink cartridges are complements. If printer prices rise sharply, what is the likely effect on demand for ink cartridges?

options.text: It shifts right.
It shifts left.
It is unaffected.
Cartridge supply automatically doubles.

questions.explanation: Higher printer prices reduce printer purchases and therefore reduce demand for the complementary cartridges.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Which change would most likely shift supply to the right?

options.text: Higher input costs
Improved production technology
Fewer sellers
An expectation of much higher future prices that encourages withholding today

questions.explanation: Better technology can lower unit costs and allow more output at each price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Why might a firm estimate a demand function?

options.text: To identify how quantity demanded responds to price and other determinants
To guarantee future profit
To remove all uncertainty
To replace customer research with accounting

questions.explanation: Demand functions help quantify relationships using experience, research and pricing evidence.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Consumers expect a product to cost more next month. What may happen to current demand?

options.text: Supply becomes perfectly elastic.
It shifts right as some purchases are brought forward.
It shifts left because future price rises.
There is only movement along supply.

questions.explanation: Expectations are a non-price determinant of current demand.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes and supply-and-demand materials

questions.stem: The number of sellers in a market increases. What happens to market supply, other things equal?

options.text: It shifts left.
Demand shifts right.
Quantity demanded falls along the curve.
It shifts right.

questions.explanation: More sellers make more output available at each price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes and supply-and-demand materials

questions.stem: What distinguishes a demand schedule from a demand curve?

options.text: The schedule is a table of price–quantity pairs; the curve graphs the same relationship.
The schedule includes supply while the curve excludes price.
The curve is always more accurate.
The schedule shows only one price.

questions.explanation: Both represent demand, in tabular and graphical forms.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes and supply-and-demand materials

questions.stem: Why must the ceteris paribus condition accompany the law of demand?

options.text: It means every determinant changes together.
It guarantees demand is linear.
It removes consumer choice.
It isolates the relationship between own price and quantity demanded.

questions.explanation: Other determinants are held constant so an own-price movement can be identified.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes and supply-and-demand materials

questions.stem: A product’s own price rises and other factors do not change. What happens on its supply curve?

options.text: There is an upward movement to a larger quantity supplied
The supply curve shifts left
The supply curve shifts right
Demand shifts right

questions.explanation: A change in the good’s own price changes quantity supplied along the existing curve.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Energy input costs rise while a product’s own price is unchanged. What does the usual supply model predict?

options.text: A movement down the existing supply curve only
A leftward supply shift
A rightward demand shift caused solely by own price
An outward supply shift from lower production cost

questions.explanation: Higher input cost reduces supply at each given selling price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 3, supply determinants

questions.stem: A new production method lowers unit cost while consumer preferences are unchanged. Which curve shifts directly?

options.text: The existing demand curve rotates to become vertical
Demand shifts left solely because production is cheaper
Supply shifts left from increased cost
Supply shifts right

questions.explanation: Lower production cost increases supply at given prices.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 3, supply determinants

questions.stem: Smartphones and mobile data plans are complements. If smartphone prices fall, what is likely to happen to demand for data plans?

options.text: Only quantity supplied changes
Demand for data plans shifts right
Demand for data plans shifts left
Supply of data plans must fall

questions.explanation: Cheaper smartphones can increase phone ownership and therefore demand for the complementary service.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: A city’s population grows while preferences and incomes are unchanged. What is the likely market-demand effect for ordinary groceries?

options.text: Market demand shifts left
Supply shifts right automatically
There is only a movement along demand
Market demand shifts right

questions.explanation: More potential buyers generally increase market demand at each price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What does “an increase in demand” mean?

options.text: The entire demand curve shifts right
Quantity demanded rises because the good’s own price falls
The supply curve shifts left
Price rises with no curve change

questions.explanation: Demand refers to the full relationship, so an increase is a rightward shift caused by a non-price determinant.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Sellers expect their product’s price to be much higher next month and can store it cheaply. What may happen to current supply?

options.text: Quantity supplied must rise at every current price
Current supply may shift left
Current supply must shift right
Current demand shifts left by definition

questions.explanation: Some sellers may withhold stock for later, reducing current supply.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Why include income and related-goods prices in an estimated demand function?

options.text: They are always controlled by the firm
They are non-price determinants that may shift demand
They define the physical production technology
They guarantee equilibrium

questions.explanation: Demand depends on more than the product’s own price, so relevant determinants help explain observed sales.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Why can a temporary price promotion help estimate demand?

options.text: It creates variation that reveals how purchases respond to price
It makes all customers identical
It proves the supply curve is vertical
It removes seasonality automatically

questions.explanation: Observed responses to planned price changes can provide evidence about the price–quantity relationship.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: A firm sees sales rise after cutting price, but a holiday occurred at the same time. What is the main analytical problem?

options.text: Supply cannot exist during holidays
Quantity demanded cannot be measured
The sales change may reflect both price and a demand shift
The law of demand has been disproved

questions.explanation: A simultaneous change in another determinant makes it hard to isolate the causal effect of price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: There are five students who are looking to buy one second-hand textbook each. Their willingness to pay is £5, £6, £8, £12 and £15, respectively. Which statement is correct?

options.text: To sell three books, the maximum price that can be charged is £8.
The student with a willingness to pay of £15 is the richest.
If a seller is one of many identical sellers and his reservation price is £8, then he is guaranteed to sell his textbook.
Their willingness to pay indicates an upward-sloping demand curve.

questions.explanation: At £8, three students are willing to buy; above £8, only two are. Willingness to pay does not reveal wealth or guarantee a sale.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 60

questions.stem: A poor wheat harvest occurred in 1845. Average prices in 1838–45 → maximum prices in 1845–48 (relative to silver) were: Austria 52.9 → 104.0 and Hungary 39.0 → 92.3, both with violent revolution in 1848; England 115.3 → 134.7 and Sweden 75.8 → 81.4, both without violent revolution. Which statement is supported?

options.text: A downward shift of the supply curve caused the price hike.
A high average price of wheat caused violent revolution.
Countries with a violent revolution necessarily had a more inelastic demand curve.
There is a positive correlation between large wheat-price hikes and the incidence of violent revolution.

questions.explanation: The price changes are about 96.6%, 136.7%, 16.8% and 7.4%, respectively. The data support an association, not proof of causation or demand elasticity.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 63

questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the major factors that shifts the supply curve when it changes?

options.text: The income of consumers
Prices of inputs used in production
The number of sellers
Sellers’ expectations about the future

questions.explanation: Consumer income shifts demand. Input costs, seller numbers and relevant expectations can shift supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 64

questions.stem: The wine industry relies on unskilled labour to pick grapes. Other things equal, an increase in immigration that increases the available labour supply and reduces labour costs will shift the supply curve of wine:

options.text: Rightwards
Leftwards
It will remain unchanged
The supply curve becomes perfectly vertical

questions.explanation: Lower labour costs make more wine profitable to supply at each price. The cost assumption makes the original question explicit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 65

questions.stem: Which factor is expected to cause the demand curve for coffee to shift to the right?

options.text: A higher tax on the sale of tea, a substitute for coffee
A fall in the manufacturing cost of coffee
A higher personal tax on the income of all consumers
An increase in the supply of coffee due to better weather

questions.explanation: A tax that raises the price of tea encourages substitution towards coffee. Coffee production costs and weather affect coffee supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 68

questions.stem: Quinoa production and prices rose following stronger overseas demand. With other factors held constant, which interpretation fits the demand-and-supply model?

options.text: Demand shifted right, and higher prices encourage other countries to increase production
Supply shifted left, and the resulting higher price benefits every buyer
Demand shifted left, and higher prices discourage production elsewhere
Demand shifted right, and the higher price necessarily benefits everyone in producing countries

questions.explanation: Higher demand explains the joint rise in price and output. Higher prices encourage additional production but hurt buyers. The charts are summarised by their relevant trend, and the demand-shift interpretation is conditional on other factors being unchanged. Source charts
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 71

questions.stem: New technology shifts the bread supply curve right/down, while demand and the number of bakeries remain unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bakeries’ marginal cost of production has fallen.
Excess demand at the original price has led to the fall in equilibrium price.
The more elastic the demand curve, the larger the fall in price.
There has been an increase in demand.

questions.explanation: The technology reduces costs. At the old price there is excess supply. The stated shift makes the diagram-based question self-contained.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 72

questions.stem: A fall in the price of a substitute raises demand for the substitute and reduces demand for takeaway pizza. At the same time, higher energy costs reduce pizza supply. Which outcome can be predicted with certainty?

options.text: Equilibrium price rises and quantity rises.
Equilibrium quantity of pizza falls; the direction of the price change is ambiguous.
Both equilibrium price and quantity necessarily fall.
Equilibrium price falls and quantity rises.

questions.explanation: The fall in pizza demand and the fall in pizza supply both reduce equilibrium quantity. The demand change puts downward pressure on price, while the supply change puts upward pressure on it, so the net price effect is ambiguous.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q7; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Market Equilibrium, Shortages & Surpluses
chapters.description: Equilibrium calculation, market adjustment and real-world comparative statics.

questions.stem: What defines market equilibrium?

options.text: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Price is zero.
Every consumer buys the same quantity.

questions.explanation: At equilibrium, planned purchases and sales coincide.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: At a price above equilibrium, what normally occurs?

options.text: A shortage
A surplus
No unsold output
Demand shifts right automatically

questions.explanation: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating downward pressure on price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: At a price below equilibrium, what normally occurs?

options.text: A surplus
A shortage
Excess supply
No pressure for adjustment

questions.explanation: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, tending to push price upward.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: Given Qd=90−2P and Qs=10+3P, what is the equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: Set Qd equal to Qs: 90−2P=10+3P, so 80=5P and P=16.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: For Qd=90−2P and Qs=10+3P, what is equilibrium quantity?
questions.explanation: Substituting P=16 gives Q=90−32=58, also 10+48=58.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Demand for student housing rises while short-run supply is constrained. What is the likely equilibrium effect?

options.text: Lower price and lower quantity
Higher price, with limited quantity expansion
Lower price and higher quantity
No price change by definition

questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift against inelastic short-run supply mainly raises equilibrium price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Suppose demand for gas shifts left while gas supply shifts right. What price effect is unambiguous?

options.text: Equilibrium price rises.
Equilibrium price falls.
Equilibrium price is unchanged.
Price becomes zero.

questions.explanation: Both changes place downward pressure on equilibrium price, though the quantity effect can be ambiguous.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: In a standard competitive model without externalities, demand shifts right/up as consumers become richer and supply shifts right/down as marginal costs fall. What follows?

options.text: Quantity traded and total surplus rise; the direction of the price change is indeterminate
Price must fall, while quantity traded must fall
Price must rise, while total surplus must fall
Quantity traded stays constant, while price must fall

questions.explanation: Price depends on the relative shifts. Both changes increase traded quantity. Higher willingness to pay and lower production costs increase the gains from trade in this model.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 73

questions.stem: What is a comparative-statics exercise?

options.text: Comparing equilibrium before and after an external change
Measuring only accounting profit
Holding every determinant fixed forever
Calculating production without prices

questions.explanation: Comparative statics traces how a shift in demand or supply changes the equilibrium.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: Why should a calculated equilibrium be interpreted rather than reported alone?

options.text: The mechanism shows which curve shifted and why price and quantity changed.
The numerical answer is always wrong.
Equilibrium has no economic meaning.
Interpretation changes the algebra.

questions.explanation: Economic reasoning links the result to incentives, shortages, surpluses and curve shifts.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: At the current price Qd=70 and Qs=50. What market condition exists?

options.text: A shortage of 20 units.
A surplus of 20 units.
Equilibrium at 60 units.
A demand shift of 120 units.

questions.explanation: Demand exceeds supply by 20, creating excess demand.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: At the current price Qd=40 and Qs=65. What market condition exists?

options.text: A supply shift of 105 units.
A surplus of 25 units.
A shortage of 25 units.
Equilibrium at 52.5 units.

questions.explanation: Supply exceeds demand by 25, creating downward price pressure.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: Z is a normal good. Its equilibrium price and quantity were €25 and 60 units in 2020. In 2021 they increased to €35 and 70 units. Other things equal, which change could explain this?

options.text: A shift of demand for Z to the right
A shift of demand for Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the right
A shift of supply of Z to the left

questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift raises both equilibrium price and quantity with unchanged upward-sloping supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 69

questions.stem: Supply decreases while demand is unchanged. What happens in the standard model?

options.text: Both price and quantity fall.
Equilibrium price rises and quantity falls.
Price falls and quantity rises.
Both price and quantity rise.

questions.explanation: A leftward supply shift makes the good scarcer at each price.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: If demand and supply both decrease, which result is certain?

options.text: Equilibrium price must rise.
Equilibrium price must fall.
Equilibrium quantity must rise.
Equilibrium quantity falls, while the price effect is ambiguous.

questions.explanation: Both shifts reduce quantity, but they push price in opposite directions.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: Why does a price below equilibrium tend to face upward pressure?

options.text: Demand and supply both become zero
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so buyers compete for limited units
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Every seller leaves the market immediately

questions.explanation: A shortage gives sellers scope to raise price and attracts additional supply.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Why does a price above equilibrium tend to face downward pressure?

options.text: Supply becomes perfectly inelastic
Unsold stock encourages sellers to reduce price
A shortage forces buyers to bid more
Demand automatically shifts right

questions.explanation: A surplus creates pressure to clear excess stock through lower prices.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Given Qd=100−4P and Qs=20+4P, what is the equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: Set demand equal to supply: 100−4P=20+4P, so 80=8P and P=10.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: For Qd=100−4P and Qs=20+4P, what is the equilibrium quantity?
questions.explanation: At P=10, both Qd and Qs equal 60.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: Z is a normal good. Its equilibrium price and quantity were €25 and 60 units in 2020. In 2021 they decreased to €15 and 50 units. Other things equal, which change could explain this?

options.text: A shift of demand for Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the right
A shift of demand for Z to the right

questions.explanation: A leftward demand shift lowers both price and quantity with unchanged supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 70

questions.stem: Supply shifts right while demand stays unchanged. What is the standard result?

options.text: Price and quantity both fall
Equilibrium price falls and quantity rises
Price and quantity both rise
Price rises and quantity falls

questions.explanation: Greater supply lowers the clearing price while allowing more units to trade.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: At a price of €12, quantity demanded is 80 and quantity supplied is 62. What is the size of the shortage?

options.text: 68 units
18 units
142 units

questions.explanation: The shortage is Qd−Qs=80−62=18 units.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: How is a surplus normally removed in a flexible-price market?

options.text: Price rises, increasing both quantities equally
Demand is legally set to zero
Supply shifts right automatically
Price falls, raising quantity demanded and reducing quantity supplied

questions.explanation: A lower price moves buyers and sellers along their curves towards the clearing quantity.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: The textbook market has demand P = 20 − 0.5Q and supply P = 2 + 0.25Q, with price in dollars. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The equilibrium price is $8.
At a price of $6, there is excess demand of 4 books.
There are sellers willing to give away their textbooks for free.
At a price of $12, all books offered for sale will be sold.

questions.explanation: 20 − 0.5Q = 2 + 0.25Q gives Q = 24 and P = 8. At 6, Qd = 28 and Qs = 16, so excess demand is 12 books. The replacement uses the matching CORE textbook-market model. Source model
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 62

questions.stem: National income increases by 20%, causing a 20% increase in houses demanded at every price. Assume demand slopes downward and the unchanged supply curve slopes upward with finite elasticity. The equilibrium number of houses traded is likely to:

options.text: Increase by less than 20%
Increase by 20%
Stay the same
Fall by less than 20%

questions.explanation: The demand shift raises price; this reduces part of the quantity increase. Perfectly elastic supply would instead allow a 20% increase; perfectly inelastic supply would leave quantity unchanged. The original omitted the supply assumption.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 67

questions.stem: More students arrive, shifting textbook demand right/up while an upward-sloping supply curve remains unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Every buyer who would have bought before the shift will still buy after it.
The more inelastic supply is, the larger the increase in quantity traded.
There has been an increase in supply.
The more elastic supply is, the smaller the price rise.

questions.explanation: Supply elasticity governs how much adjustment occurs through quantity rather than price.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 85

questions.stem: A competitive market has demand P=30−0.2Q. Supply changes from S₀: P=0.1Q to S₁: P=6+0.1Q, while demand is unchanged. Using the diagram and equations, what are the new equilibrium price and quantity?

options.text: P=€10 per unit; Q=100 units.
P=€14 per unit; Q=80 units.
P=€16 per unit; Q=100 units.
P=€8 per unit; Q=80 units.

questions.explanation: Equate demand with the replacement supply: 30−0.2Q=6+0.1Q. Thus Q=80 and P=€14. The original equilibrium was Q=100 and P=€10.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, Section P2; latest lecture-based practice variation. Numerical models and diagrams are illustrative, not lecturer measurements.

questions.stem: Demand is Qd=150−5P and supply is Qs=30+3P, where P is euros per unit. Which equilibrium pair is correct?
questions.explanation: Set 150−5P=30+3P: 120=8P, so P=€15. Both schedules give Q=75.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #3 — equilibrium algebra and adjustment; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c814a9229fa9424179662

questions.stem: A market has demand Qd=150−5P and supply Qs=30+3P. If price is held at €10, what is the market imbalance?

options.text: Excess supply of 40 units
Excess demand of 60 units
Excess supply of 100 units
Excess demand of 40 units

questions.explanation: At P=10, Qd=100 and Qs=60. The shortage is Qd−Qs=40 units.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #3 — equilibrium algebra and adjustment; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c814a9229fa9424179662

questions.stem: Supply is Qs=30+3P. Demand changes from Qd=150−5P to Qd=190−5P, with price in euros per unit. What are the new equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Use the new demand schedule: 190−5P=30+3P, so P=20 and Q=90. The rightward demand shift raises both equilibrium values.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #3 — equilibrium algebra and adjustment; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c814a9229fa9424179662

questions.stem: Aldi estimates demand Qd = 150 − 3P and supply Qs = 30 + 2P for a wine. A €5 per-bottle tax on suppliers changes supply to Qs = 30 + 2(P − 5). What are the new consumer price and equilibrium quantity?

options.text: €26 and 72 bottles.
€28 and 66 bottles.
€24 and 78 bottles.
€26 and 82 bottles.

questions.explanation: After the tax, Qs = 30 + 2(P − 5) = 20 + 2P. Equating supply and demand gives 150 − 3P = 20 + 2P, hence P = €26 and Q = 72. P is the consumer price; suppliers receive €21 after tax.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q5; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.
