questions.stem: In the figure, both demand and supply shift vertically upwards by €12 at every quantity (D0→D1 and S0→S1). What happens to equilibrium?

options.text: Equilibrium price rises while equilibrium quantity remains unchanged.
Equilibrium quantity rises while price is unchanged.
Price falls and quantity rises.
Both price and quantity are unchanged.

questions.explanation: Raising both inverse demand and inverse supply by the same €12 leaves their intersection’s quantity unchanged and raises its price by €12. In the chart, Q remains 24 while P rises from €31.20 to €43.20.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q6; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

image.alt: Price (€) against quantity, with downward-sloping D0 and D1 and upward-sloping S0 and S1; D1 and S1 lie €12 above their corresponding original curves.

questions.stem: A market has Qd = 120 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 30. The government imposes a binding maximum price of €24. What shortage results?

options.text: 60 units.
30 units.
15 units.
0 units.

questions.explanation: At the maximum price of €24, Qd = 120 − 2(24) = 72 and Qs = 3(24) − 30 = 42. The shortage is 72 − 42 = 30 units.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q8; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Allocation, Surplus & Limits of Markets
chapters.description: Consumer and producer surplus, allocation mechanisms and limitations of competitive outcomes.

questions.stem: What is consumer surplus?

options.text: Price paid minus willingness to pay
Willingness to pay minus price paid
Revenue minus total cost
Price minus marginal cost for the seller

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the gain buyers receive when they pay less than their maximum willingness to pay.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: What is producer surplus?

options.text: Willingness to pay minus price
Price received minus the seller’s marginal cost
Total cost minus revenue
Tax revenue minus subsidy

questions.explanation: Producer surplus measures the seller’s gain above the cost of supplying the marginal unit.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: Under standard competitive assumptions, why is equilibrium described as efficient?

options.text: It maximises total consumer and producer surplus.
It guarantees equal incomes.
It eliminates all external costs.
It prevents every shortage by law.

questions.explanation: Competitive equilibrium maximises gains from trade when the model’s assumptions hold.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: Which condition most directly weakens the claim that market equilibrium maximises social welfare?

options.text: External costs imposed on third parties
Many informed buyers and sellers
Voluntary exchange
Prices that reflect marginal cost

questions.explanation: Externalities mean private market prices omit costs or benefits borne outside the transaction.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Which is an allocation mechanism other than ordinary market pricing?

options.text: First-come, first-served queueing
Setting Qd equal to Qs
Calculating present value
Reducing fixed cost

questions.explanation: Scarce items can be allocated by queues, eligibility, loyalty rules or other mechanisms.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Why might a performer deliberately price tickets below the resale-market clearing price?

options.text: To guarantee there is no shortage
To pursue brand, community or long-term relationship goals
Because lower prices always maximise immediate revenue
Because resale is impossible

questions.explanation: A firm may value access, goodwill or long-run strategy alongside immediate revenue.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: What is a likely consequence of underpricing a popular fixed-capacity event?

options.text: A surplus of unsold tickets
Excess demand and non-price rationing
An automatic increase in venue capacity
Demand shifts left immediately

questions.explanation: Below-equilibrium pricing creates a shortage, so queues, lotteries or resale may allocate tickets.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Why can a resale market emerge after tickets are underpriced?

options.text: Some buyers value tickets more than the official price and can trade with initial holders.
The original supply curve disappears.
Every buyer has identical willingness to pay.
Resale guarantees equity.

questions.explanation: Differences in willingness to pay create gains from further exchange after the initial allocation.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the relationship between efficiency and fairness?

options.text: An efficient outcome is necessarily fair.
Fairness is a separate judgement from whether gains from trade are exhausted.
Fairness can be calculated only from supply.
Efficiency requires equal allocations.

questions.explanation: Total-surplus efficiency does not determine whether the distribution is socially acceptable.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 notes

questions.stem: When is market-price allocation most likely to need supplementation?

options.text: When externalities, market power, poor information or distributional concerns are important
Whenever demand slopes downward
Whenever firms estimate demand
Whenever price equals marginal cost

questions.explanation: Market outcomes may not serve social welfare when key competitive assumptions fail or equity concerns matter.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: Mary is willing to pay at most €40 for a bracelet. She buys it for €22.50. What consumer surplus does she gain?
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price = €40 − €22.50 = €17.50.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 78

questions.stem: A seller receives €18 for a unit with marginal cost €12. What is producer surplus?
questions.explanation: Producer surplus equals price received minus marginal cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: Why can a queue allocate scarce goods inefficiently?

options.text: Queues reveal marginal cost perfectly.
Time costs may replace money prices and items may not reach those valuing them most.
Queues always increase supply.
Waiting has no opportunity cost.

questions.explanation: Non-price rationing can consume resources and misallocate goods.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: Why might market power reduce total surplus?

options.text: It eliminates barriers to entry.
It makes demand perfectly elastic.
A powerful seller can restrict output and raise price above the competitive level.
It guarantees price equals marginal cost.

questions.explanation: Restricted output can block mutually beneficial trades.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: On a standard demand-and-supply diagram, where is consumer surplus for units traded?

options.text: Above the demand curve only
Below the demand curve and above the market price
Above the supply curve and below the market price
Below both curves

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and the price actually paid.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: On a standard demand-and-supply diagram, where is producer surplus for units traded?

options.text: Below the supply curve only
Above the supply curve and below the market price
Below the demand curve and above the market price
Above both curves

questions.explanation: Producer surplus is the gap between the price received and the minimum supply price or marginal cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What is total surplus in the basic market model?

options.text: Consumer surplus plus producer surplus
Revenue plus accounting cost
Price multiplied by shortage
Consumer income plus tax revenue only

questions.explanation: Total surplus adds the gains from trade received by buyers and sellers.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: How can an unpriced pollution cost distort market allocation?

options.text: The market may produce more than the socially efficient quantity
The market always produces too little
Demand and supply cease to exist
Consumer surplus automatically equals zero

questions.explanation: If external costs are omitted from private decisions, the market price understates the full social cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: A seller reduces traded output below the competitive quantity while raising price. Why can total surplus fall?

options.text: Every gain transferred to the seller is an extra social gain
A higher price necessarily raises every buyer’s surplus
Some mutually beneficial trades no longer occur
Only fixed costs determine total gains from trade

questions.explanation: Restricting trade can reduce total gains, not merely redistribute them.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5, limits of markets; Market Structure slides

questions.stem: Buyers cannot distinguish high-quality products from low-quality ones before purchase. Which market limitation is most direct?

options.text: An increase in the number of external schemas
Information asymmetry
Perfect knowledge of all product characteristics
A movement along the supply curve caused only by the product price

questions.explanation: Unequal access to relevant quality information can undermine market choices.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 4–5, market limitations

questions.stem: Why is waiting time a real cost of queue allocation?

options.text: People spend time that could have been used elsewhere
Queues create unlimited supply
Waiting raises every buyer’s willingness to pay
Time has no opportunity cost

questions.explanation: Time sacrificed in a queue is an opportunity cost even when the money price is low.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What is a trade-off of allocating a scarce service by eligibility rules?

options.text: It may improve fairness but exclude some high-value users or add administration
It always maximises total surplus
It eliminates the need for information
It is identical to auction allocation

questions.explanation: Eligibility can target need, but this may sacrifice some efficiency and create screening costs.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What is a possible purpose of loyalty-based ticket access?

options.text: Reward committed customers and limit access by resellers
Guarantee the highest possible market price
Remove all excess demand
Make tickets a public good

questions.explanation: Loyalty rules use past engagement rather than willingness to pay as the allocation criterion.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: What can high resale prices reveal after an event is underpriced?

options.text: The event has no scarcity
Some buyers’ willingness to pay exceeds the original price
The original supply was unlimited
Consumer demand was zero

questions.explanation: Resale prices provide evidence of strong excess demand, though the resulting allocation may raise fairness concerns.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures 3–5 and reviewed module notes

questions.stem: For straight-line bread demand and supply curves, keep their intersection (equilibrium price and output) unchanged while varying slopes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A less elastic demand curve leads to smaller consumer surplus.
A less elastic supply curve leads to larger producer surplus.
A more elastic demand curve leads to smaller producer surplus when supply is unchanged.
Consumer and producer surplus do not depend on curve elasticities.

questions.explanation: Steeper supply increases the area between price and supply to the left of equilibrium. The linear-curve assumption makes the original diagram-based comparison precise.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 86

questions.stem: The figure shows a competitive market. At the equilibrium, what is consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: The graph shows equilibrium at Q = 20 and P = €40, with a demand-price intercept of €80. Consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 20 × (€80 − €40) = €400.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q12; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

image.alt: Price (€) against quantity: downward-sloping demand from €80 at zero quantity to zero at 40; upward-sloping supply from €20 at zero to €60 at 40; dotted price line at €40.

chapters.title: Consumers — Marginal Utility & Demand Elasticities
chapters.description: Delivered consumer reasoning and verified consumer slides; no uncovered indifference-curve derivations.

questions.stem: What does marginal utility measure?

options.text: The additional satisfaction from one extra unit consumed
All satisfaction from every unit already consumed
The product’s total market revenue
The cost of producing one more unit

questions.explanation: Marginal utility is an increment in satisfaction, unlike total utility.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 3

questions.stem: If total utility rises from 100 to 170 after a second unit, what is that unit’s marginal utility?
questions.explanation: The additional utility is 170 − 100 = 70.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 3; new practice example

questions.stem: What does diminishing positive marginal utility imply?

options.text: Every additional unit adds exactly the same satisfaction
The price of every unit must decrease
Total utility must immediately fall
Total utility still rises, but each additional unit adds less

questions.explanation: Diminishing marginal utility concerns the increment; a positive increment still raises the total.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 3

questions.stem: Good X offers marginal utility 60 at price €3; good Y offers 80 at price €8. Which offers more utility per euro at those margins?

options.text: Y, with 80 per euro
Both offer 10 per euro
Neither can be compared because prices differ
X, with 20 per euro

questions.explanation: Compare MU/P: X = 60/3 = 20 and Y = 80/8 = 10.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 4; new practice example

questions.stem: At an interior optimum with diminishing marginal benefits, a consumer’s satisfaction is maximised when marginal benefit per euro is equal across goods because:

options.text: Any small reallocation of expenditure towards either good would fail to improve satisfaction.
Any shift in consumption towards either good violates the budget constraint.
Her preferences become invalid when marginal benefits per euro differ.
Unequal ratios imply that she has insufficient income to maximise satisfaction.

questions.explanation: If one good yielded more benefit per euro, shifting spending towards it would improve satisfaction. The interior-optimum assumption avoids corner-solution exceptions.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 76

questions.stem: A buyer values a unit at €35 and pays €20. What is their consumer surplus on that unit?
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay less the actual price.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 5; new practice example

questions.stem: What is the basic price-elasticity-of-demand ratio?

options.text: Change in price in euro divided by total utility
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
Percentage change in income divided by quantity supplied
Total revenue divided by total cost

questions.explanation: PED is a relative responsiveness measure; absolute magnitude is used for elastic/inelastic classification.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 12–19

questions.stem: A 10% price rise causes quantity demanded to fall 25%, using the same percentage basis. What is absolute PED?
questions.explanation: The magnitude is 25%/10% = 2.5, indicating elastic demand.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 12–19; new practice example

questions.stem: A 10% price rise causes quantity demanded to fall 4%. How is demand classified over that change?

options.text: Elastic
Perfectly elastic
Inelastic
Unit elastic

questions.explanation: The absolute ratio is 4/10 = 0.4, less than one.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 19; new practice example

questions.stem: How does unit-elastic demand compare quantity and price percentage changes?

options.text: Quantity changes infinitely
Quantity never changes when price changes
The euro price change equals the unit quantity change
Their absolute percentage changes are equal

questions.explanation: An absolute PED of one means equal proportional responsiveness.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 19

questions.stem: In the standard demand model, what does perfectly inelastic demand mean?

options.text: Any price rise eliminates every purchase
Demand is horizontal
Quantity demanded does not respond to price changes
Quantity responds proportionately more than price

questions.explanation: PED is zero and the conventional demand curve is vertical.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 19–21

questions.stem: Why can a straight demand curve have changing elasticity along it?

options.text: The curve must secretly be shifting
Elasticity and slope are always numerically identical
Constant absolute slope does not mean constant proportional responsiveness
Every straight demand curve is perfectly elastic

questions.explanation: Elasticity uses percentages; their bases change along a constant-slope curve.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 18

questions.stem: For demand that is inelastic over a price change, what normally happens to revenue after a price rise?

options.text: Revenue falls because quantity necessarily falls more than price rises
Revenue is always unchanged
Revenue rises because quantity falls proportionately less
Revenue and profit become identical

questions.explanation: TR = P×Q; the proportionate price increase dominates the smaller quantity reduction.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 22

questions.stem: For demand that is elastic over a price change, what normally happens to revenue after a price reduction?

options.text: Revenue rises because quantity increases proportionately more
Revenue must fall in the same proportion as price
Revenue is unrelated to quantity
Quantity remains fixed

questions.explanation: With elastic demand, the proportionate quantity response dominates the price reduction.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 22–26

questions.stem: Which factor tends to make demand more price-elastic, other things equal?

options.text: More close substitutes
A smaller need to consider price
Fewer possible alternatives
Less time to adjust

questions.explanation: Close substitutes make switching easier.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slide 27

questions.stem: Holding other forces constant, a rise in motor-fuel prices produces a larger fall in quantity demanded over ten years than immediately because:

options.text: Buyers are more sensitive to price changes when given more time to respond.
Long-run demand is perfectly inelastic because consumers have more time to adjust
Buyers are less sensitive to price changes when given more time to react.
Buyers necessarily have substantially more income after ten years.

questions.explanation: People have more time to change vehicles, travel habits or location, making long-run demand more elastic.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 83

questions.stem: What does positive cross-price elasticity between two goods usually indicate?

options.text: Both must have perfectly inelastic demand
They are substitutes
They are complements
Both must be inferior goods

questions.explanation: A rise in one good’s price increases demand for the other when they are substitutes.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 29–30

questions.stem: Demand for printers falls when ink prices rise. What sign would the cross-price elasticity of printer demand with respect to ink price have?

options.text: Necessarily infinite
Positive
Negative
Necessarily zero

questions.explanation: Complementary goods move in opposite directions for this cross-price relationship.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 29–30

questions.stem: A 10% income rise raises quantity demanded by 5%. What is income elasticity using those percentage changes?

options.text: 0.5, indicating a normal good
−0.5, indicating an inferior good
5, indicating unit elasticity
2, indicating an inferior good

questions.explanation: Income elasticity is 5/10 = 0.5; its positive sign indicates a normal good.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 34–35; new practice example

questions.stem: Quantity demanded falls as income rises, other things equal. What does the negative income elasticity indicate?

options.text: A good with no demand
An inferior good
A perfectly elastic supply curve
A substitute for every other good

questions.explanation: The income-elasticity sign distinguishes normal from inferior goods; inferior is not a quality judgement.
questions.source: EC2204 Consumers and Incentives slide deck; Lectures 6–7; slides 34–35

questions.stem: A restaurant increases its pizza price from €12 to €15. Sales fall from 200 to 160 pizzas per week. Using initial values as the percentage-change base, what is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Quantity change: (160 − 200)/200 = −20%. Price change: (15 − 12)/12 = 25%. PED = −20/25 = −0.8. Using the midpoint method instead gives −1.0; the method must be specified.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 74

questions.stem: A drought reduces the available quantity of wheat by 20%. If PED is −0.5, use the percentage-change elasticity approximation to estimate the price increase needed for quantity demanded to fall by 20%.
questions.explanation: %ΔQ = PED × %ΔP, so %ΔP = −20%/−0.5 = 40%. This is the introductory approximation, not an exact large-change prediction from a constant-elasticity demand function.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 75

questions.stem: Total expected extra marks from studying for 1–5 hours are 10, 14, 18, 21 and 23; total marks lost through tiredness are 0, 3, 7, 12 and 18. Which pair of durations ties for the highest net expected marks?

options.text: 2 and 3 hours
1 and 2 hours
3 and 4 hours
4 and 5 hours

questions.explanation: Net benefits: 1 hour = 10 − 0 = 10; 2 = 14 − 3 = 11; 3 = 18 − 7 = 11; 4 = 21 − 12 = 9; 5 = 23 − 18 = 5. Both 2 and 3 hours maximise net marks. The third hour has MB = MC = 4, so it adds zero net benefit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 77

questions.stem: The price of bags rises from €11 to €13 and quantity demanded falls from 56 to 52. A further table row gives €15 and 44 bags. Using the initial point (€11, 56) and the €11 → €13 interval, what is the absolute price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: ΔQ = −4 and ΔP = 2. Initial-point estimate: (−4/2) × (11/56) = −0.392857, absolute value ≈ 0.39. The midpoint/arc value is about 0.44, which was incorrectly mixed into the original point-elasticity question.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 79

questions.stem: Last year John bought 50 pounds of mincemeat when household income was €40,000. This year income was €30,000 and he bought 60 pounds. All else constant, his income elasticity is:

options.text: Negative, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Negative, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.

questions.explanation: Quantity rises as income falls. Using initial values gives (10/50)/(−10,000/40,000) = −0.8.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 80

questions.stem: In any market where units sell at a common price, total revenue is price:

options.text: Multiplied by quantity
Divided by the price elasticity of demand
Multiplied by quantity minus production costs
Plus quantity

questions.explanation: TR = P × Q. Subtracting costs gives profit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 81

questions.stem: The cross-price elasticity of food demand with respect to the price of entertainment is −0.7. If entertainment prices rise by 20%, the percentage-change approximation predicts that food quantity demanded:

options.text: Rises by 0.14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are complements.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 0.14%, and the goods are complements.

questions.explanation: %ΔQfood = −0.7 × 20% = −14%. A negative cross-price elasticity identifies complements.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 82

questions.stem: You and your housemate each eat three packets of Pot Noodles weekly. After your incomes rise, you buy more while your housemate buys fewer and substitutes preferred foods. Your income elasticity and your housemate’s are, respectively:

options.text: Approaching infinity and zero
Zero and approaching infinity
Positive and negative
Negative and positive

questions.explanation: The same product can be normal for one person and inferior for another.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 84

questions.stem: Use the table of product Y’s price and product X’s quantity demanded. Other influences are held constant. Using initial-value percentage changes, what is X’s cross-price elasticity with respect to Y’s price, and what relationship does it indicate?

options.text: −1.5; complements.
+0.67; substitutes.
−0.67; complements.
+1.5; substitutes.

questions.explanation: Quantity demanded of X rises 30/200=15%; Y’s price rises 0.80/8=10%. Cross-price elasticity is 15%/10%=+1.5. The positive sign is consistent with substitution.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, Section P3; latest lecture-based practice variation. Numerical models and diagrams are illustrative, not lecturer measurements.

artifact.title: Two-product observations
artifact.html:
ObservationBeforeAfter
Price of Y€8.00€8.80
Quantity demanded of X200 units230 units

Illustrative observations; other influences are held constant. Use initial-value percentage changes, not midpoint percentages.

questions.stem: Price rises from €20 to €24 and quantity demanded falls from 150 to 105 units. Using initial values as the percentage-change bases, what is signed PED and its classification?

options.text: −0.67; inelastic
+1.5; elastic
−1.5; elastic
−0.3; inelastic

questions.explanation: Quantity changes by −45/150=−30%; price changes by 4/20=20%. PED=−30%/20%=−1.5. Its magnitude exceeds one, so demand is elastic over the stated change.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures #6–7 — initial-value elasticity methods; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8121ad09cf2c3b4cd8c7 ; https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8112a715ce63d7ec737b

questions.stem: The price of Y rises from €10 to €12 while quantity demanded of X falls from 80 to 72 units, other things equal. Using initial-value percentages, what is X’s cross-price elasticity with respect to Y’s price, and what relationship does it indicate?

options.text: +0.5; substitutes
−2; complements
+2; substitutes
−0.5; complements

questions.explanation: X quantity changes by −8/80=−10%; Y price changes by 2/10=20%. The ratio is −0.5, whose negative sign indicates complements.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures #6–7 — initial-value elasticity methods; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8121ad09cf2c3b4cd8c7 ; https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8112a715ce63d7ec737b

questions.stem: Income rises from €2,000 to €2,200 and quantity demanded rises from 50 to 54 units, other things equal. Using initial-value percentages, what is income elasticity and the good’s classification over this change?

options.text: −0.8; inferior
+0.8; normal
+1.25; normal
+0.08; normal

questions.explanation: Quantity rises by 4/50=8% and income by 200/2,000=10%, giving +0.8. A positive elasticity identifies a normal good; it does not need to exceed one.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures #6–7 — initial-value elasticity methods; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8121ad09cf2c3b4cd8c7 ; https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8112a715ce63d7ec737b

questions.stem: A supplier cuts price from €20 to €18; sales rise from 100 to 130 units. Using the original price and quantity as the base for percentage changes, which combination is closest?

options.text: PED ≈ −0.81; total revenue increases.
PED ≈ −1.50; total revenue falls.
PED ≈ −3.00; total revenue increases.
PED ≈ −3.00; total revenue falls.

questions.explanation: The original-base quantity change is +30%, and the price change is −10%, giving PED = −3. Revenue rises from €20 × 100 = €2,000 to €18 × 130 = €2,340.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q9; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

questions.stem: A restaurant raises menu prices by 8%. Quantity demanded falls by 4%, while average variable cost per meal is unchanged. Which statement is defensible?

options.text: Profit necessarily rises by exactly 4%.
Demand is elastic and revenue must fall.
Revenue must fall because demand slopes downward.
Revenue increases approximately, but the effect on profit cannot be established without cost and quantity information.

questions.explanation: Revenue changes by a factor of 1.08 × 0.96 = 1.0368, an increase of 3.68%. Option D is the best available answer because the stem does not hold fixed or other costs constant. If fixed costs were unchanged and unit variable cost were non-negative and unchanged, profit would rise: revenue increases while total variable cost falls. The exact profit change cannot be calculated from the supplied information.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q10; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

questions.stem: The price of Brand A coffee increases by 12%; sales of Brand B coffee rise by 9%; sales of biscuits fall by 6%. Using the simple percentage-change method, which is correct?

options.text: Cross-price elasticity of B with respect to A is −0.75, suggesting complements.
Cross-price elasticity of B with respect to A is +0.75, suggesting substitutes.
Own-price elasticity of A is +1.33, implying a Giffen good.
Income elasticity of biscuits is −0.50, suggesting an inferior good.

questions.explanation: The cross-price elasticity of Brand B with respect to Brand A’s price is 9%/12% = +0.75. A positive cross-price elasticity is consistent with substitutes. The biscuit response concerns cross-price, not income, elasticity.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q11; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

questions.stem: A student values successive café lunches at €16, €13, €10 and €7, and each lunch costs €9. Assuming independent marginal values and no other constraints, how many lunches maximise consumer surplus?

options.text: Three lunches.
One lunch.
Four lunches.
Two lunches.

questions.explanation: The first three lunches have marginal values above their €9 price, adding €7, €4 and €1 to surplus. The fourth lunch would reduce surplus by €2, so three lunches maximise it.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q13; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Sellers — Production, Costs & Output Choice
chapters.description: Lectures 7–8 and seller slides: marginal products, costs, profits, revenue and supply response.

questions.stem: A firm has accounting profit of €30,000 and implicit opportunity costs of €40,000. What is its economic profit?
questions.explanation: Economic profit deducts implicit costs as well as financial costs.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 3; new practice example

questions.stem: In the production function A×f(K,L), what do K and L represent?

options.text: Revenue and market price
Demand and supply curves
Capital and labour inputs
Cost and total profit

questions.explanation: The delivered production-function discussion identifies technology A, capital K and labour L.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 5; Lecture 8

questions.stem: What is marginal product?

options.text: The change in output from an additional unit of input
The total selling price of all units
The change in profit from altering price
The average fixed cost per worker

questions.explanation: Marginal product concerns incremental output from input, not marginal cost or revenue.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 7

questions.stem: Output rises from 80 to 95 when one more worker is added. What is that worker’s marginal product?

options.text: 15 units
95 units
175 units
80 units

questions.explanation: The increment is 95−80 = 15 units.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 7; new practice example

questions.stem: If marginal product remains positive but is diminishing, what happens to total output?

options.text: It stays exactly constant
It rises by progressively smaller increments
It rises by progressively larger increments
It must fall immediately

questions.explanation: Positive marginal product adds output; diminishing means the amount added is falling.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 6–7

questions.stem: What can cause diminishing marginal returns in the short run?

options.text: A guarantee that every input expands proportionately
The absence of any production limit
Bottlenecks as extra workers share fixed resources
A rule that every new worker has no skill

questions.explanation: The deck identifies bottlenecks and coordination costs as reasons additional workers contribute less.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 7

questions.stem: Which definition best captures the short run in cost analysis?

options.text: A period of exactly one calendar month
A period in which some inputs are fixed
A period in which revenue is necessarily zero
A period in which every input is freely variable

questions.explanation: The short/long-run distinction is about input adjustability, not one universal time length.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 8; Lecture 8

questions.stem: What distinguishes the long run?

options.text: Every firm must earn a positive profit
Prices are fixed by law
All inputs can be varied
Only labour can change

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes long-run adjustment of both fixed and variable resources.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slide 8

questions.stem: Fixed cost is €200 and variable cost is €300 at output 100. What is total cost?
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 8–15; new practice example

questions.stem: At output 100 with total cost €500, what is average total cost?

options.text: €500 per unit
€100 per unit
€0.20 per unit
€5 per unit

questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 9–15; new practice example

questions.stem: At output 100 with fixed cost €200, what is average fixed cost?

options.text: €100 per unit
€2 per unit
€200 per unit
€0.50 per unit

questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 9–15; new practice example

questions.stem: As positive output rises, average fixed cost:

options.text: Remains the same
Rises
Falls
Cannot be determined

questions.explanation: AFC = FC/Q; an unchanged fixed cost is spread over more units.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 91

questions.stem: Total cost rises from €500 to €560 when output rises from 100 to 120. What is average marginal cost over this batch?

options.text: €20 per extra unit
€60 per extra unit
€28 per extra unit
€3 per extra unit

questions.explanation: ΔTC/ΔQ = 60/20 = €3; the whole batch’s extra cost is not the per-unit cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 9–16; new practice example

questions.stem: If marginal cost is below average total cost, an increase in output causes average total cost to:

options.text: Be impossible to determine
Stay the same
Fall
Rise

questions.explanation: Adding units that cost less than the current average lowers that average.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 96

questions.stem: In perfect competition, why is marginal revenue equal to price for an individual firm?

options.text: The firm is a price taker and can sell additional output at the market price
The firm chooses the market price
The firm has no costs
Demand is perfectly inelastic

questions.explanation: A price-taking firm receives the same market price for an extra unit, so MR = P.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 59

questions.stem: For a perfectly competitive firm that operates in the short run, an interior profit-maximising output on the rising part of MC satisfies:

options.text: Marginal cost = average total cost
Price = average total cost
Marginal revenue = price = marginal cost
Price = marginal cost = average total cost

questions.explanation: P = MR = MC is the output rule, provided operating covers variable costs. Equality with ATC is not required in the short run. The original four options omitted the general correct rule.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 94

questions.stem: A firm has selected output using MR=MC, but price is below ATC there. What does this imply?

options.text: Revenue must be identical to producer surplus
MR=MC guarantees positive profit
The chosen output can still involve an economic loss
Fixed costs must be zero

questions.explanation: Profit depends on total revenue relative to total cost, or P relative to ATC at that quantity.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 2, 4, 9–19; Lecture 8

questions.stem: What generally makes supply more price-elastic?

options.text: No inventory and no opportunity to alter production
A fixed capacity that cannot change
More adjustment time and easier access to extra productive resources
An inability to hire workers

questions.explanation: Inventory, hiring flexibility and time increase responsiveness in the seller deck.
questions.source: EC2204 Sellers and Incentives slides; Lectures 7–8; slides 22–23

questions.stem: A professional leaves a €120,000 salary to start a business. Which cost is most relevant to the economist but may not appear in the firm's accounts?

options.text: The owner's forgone €120,000 salary
The firm's rent
The firm's electricity bill
The firm's advertising cost

questions.explanation: The forgone salary is an implicit opportunity cost.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 55

questions.stem: For an audit office, why might a partner's salary be treated differently as a fixed or variable cost?

options.text: Because the classification can depend on the time horizon and how the partner's workload changes with output
Because all salaries are always fixed
Because partner salaries are never costs
Because fixed costs always change with output

questions.explanation: Cost classification depends on the relevant time horizon and whether the expense varies with output.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 56

questions.stem: A firm's total cost rises from €10,000 to €10,600 when output rises from 100 to 120 units. What is the marginal cost per additional unit?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 57

questions.stem: At the current output, a firm's marginal revenue is €900 and marginal cost is €700. What should the firm do if it wants to increase profit?

options.text: Increase output
Reduce output
Keep output unchanged because MR is irrelevant
Exit the industry immediately

questions.explanation: MR − MC = €900 − €700 = €200 for an additional unit, so expanding output can raise profit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 58

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. Labour is the only variable input. What wage is paid per worker?
questions.explanation: VC/workers = €10/1 = €20/2 = €10 per worker.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 87

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. When which worker is employed do diminishing marginal returns begin?

options.text: Fourth
Sixth
Second
Third

questions.explanation: Marginal products for workers 1–8 are 25, 30, 31, 24, 20, 15, 10 and 5. The first decline is from 31 to 24 with the fourth worker.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 88

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. What is marginal cost per additional unit over the increase in output from 25 to 55 units?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 89

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. The firm is perfectly competitive, market price is €0.50 and fixed costs are unavoidable. Which pair of listed outputs maximises short-run profit?

options.text: 110 and 130 units
55 and 86 units
86 and 110 units
145 and 155 units

questions.explanation: At 110: TR = 0.50 × 110 = €55; TC = 150 + 40 = €190; profit = −€135. At 130: TR = €65; TC = €200; profit = −€135. Net revenue TR − VC is €15 at both outputs; other table outputs yield less. Moving from 110 to 130 adds €10 revenue and €10 cost. Both maximise profit;
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 90

questions.stem: When land prices increase from €6,000 to €10,000 per acre but acreage supplied is unchanged, the price elasticity of supply over this change is:

options.text: Greater than 1

questions.explanation: %ΔQs = 0, so PES = 0: perfectly inelastic supply over the observed range. The original stem asked for a property of supply but offered bare numbers.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 92

questions.stem: According to marginal analysis, optimal decision-making involves:

options.text: Expanding an activity until total benefit is zero
Taking actions whenever marginal benefit is positive
Taking actions only if marginal cost is zero
Taking actions while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost; being indifferent to an increment when they are equal

questions.explanation: Compare additional benefit with additional cost. Equality adds zero net benefit and can produce tied optima.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 95

questions.stem: A business earns €160,000 revenue and pays €100,000 explicit costs. Its owner’s forgone salary is €70,000, the only implicit cost. What are accounting profit and economic profit, respectively?
questions.explanation: Accounting profit = €160,000 − €100,000 = €60,000. Economic profit also deducts the €70,000 forgone salary, giving −€10,000.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c811ea8fbfc99e722680a

questions.stem: At Q=200, fixed cost is €600 and total variable cost is €1,400. Which set gives AFC, AVC and ATC, respectively?

options.text: €3, €7 and €10 per unit
€7, €3 and €10 per unit
€3, €10 and €7 per unit

questions.explanation: AFC=600/200=€3; AVC=1,400/200=€7; ATC=(600+1,400)/200=€10 per unit. Total cost must not be confused with cost per unit.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c811ea8fbfc99e722680a

questions.stem: With capital fixed, hiring one more worker increases output from 240 to 280 units and total cost from €1,800 to €1,920. What are that worker’s marginal product and the marginal cost per extra output unit over this interval?

options.text: 40 units and €120 per unit
280 units and €3 per unit
40 units and €3 per unit
120 units and €40 per unit

questions.explanation: The worker adds 280−240=40 units. The additional cost is €120, so marginal cost over this batch is €120/40=€3 per unit.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c811ea8fbfc99e722680a

questions.stem: A price-taking firm can produce Q=0, 1, 2 or 3 units. Total costs are €50, €62, €80 and €106, respectively. Price is €20 per unit and the €50 fixed cost is unavoidable. Which listed output maximises short-run profit?

options.text: 0 units
1 unit
3 units
2 units

questions.explanation: Profits at Q=0,1,2,3 are −€50, −€42, −€40 and −€46. Q=2 yields the smallest loss and therefore the highest profit; producing nothing still incurs fixed cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c811ea8fbfc99e722680a

questions.stem: A Cork food producer increases the price received per unit from €10 to €14. Quantity supplied rises from 80 to 110 units per week. Using the original price and quantity as the base for percentage changes, what is the price elasticity of supply (PES), and how should it be classified?

options.text: PES ≈ 0.94; supply is inelastic.
PES ≈ 1.07; supply is elastic.
PES ≈ 0.38; supply is inelastic.
PES ≈ −0.94; supply is inelastic.

questions.explanation: Using original values, percentage quantity change is 30/80 = 37.5% and percentage price change is 4/10 = 40%. PES = 37.5%/40% = 0.9375 ≈ 0.94, which is inelastic because it is below one.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q19; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

questions.stem: The figure shows a price-taking firm with P=MR=€14. Using its marginal cost curve, which output maximises short-run profit (assuming the firm operates)?

options.text: 14 units.
10 units.
24 units.
20 units.

questions.explanation: For an operating price-taking firm, the profit-maximising output is where rising MC equals P = MR. In the graph MC meets €14 at Q = 20. AVC is below price there, so operating is consistent with the stated assumption even though ATC is above price.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q14; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

image.alt: Cost and revenue in €/unit against output: rising MC and AVC, U-shaped ATC and a horizontal P = MR line at €14. Output ticks run from 0 to 30.

questions.stem: A bakery’s total cost rises from €1,200 at 100 loaves to €1,260 at 110 loaves. Average total cost at 100 loaves is €12. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Average total cost at 110 loaves must exceed €12.
Marginal cost over the extra ten loaves is €6 per loaf, below initial ATC, so ATC falls over that range.
Fixed costs necessarily increase by €60.
Marginal cost is €60 per loaf, above ATC.

questions.explanation: The additional ten loaves cost €60, so marginal cost over that range is €60/10 = €6 per loaf. This is below initial ATC of €12. New ATC is €1,260/110 ≈ €11.45, which is lower.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q15; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Market Structure — Competition & Market Power
chapters.description: Verified Lecture 9 slides, including later slide-only sections; not a claim that all sections were delivered in class.

questions.stem: Which combination most closely describes perfect competition?

options.text: Many sellers, homogeneous products and free entry and exit
One supplier, a unique product and high entry barriers
Many differentiated sellers with strong individual price control
Few dominant firms with strategic interdependence

questions.explanation: These are the deck’s core perfect-competition characteristics.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 5

questions.stem: Assume a bakery is a price taker in a perfectly competitive bread market. Market demand slopes down; the bakery has fixed costs and rising marginal cost. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bakery can ensure that its price exceeds average cost.
The bakery faces a flat demand curve at the market price.
The bakery’s supply curve is horizontal.
The bakery always earns positive economic rent.

questions.explanation: The firm can sell at the given market price, so its own demand is horizontal. Merely having many bakeries would not establish price-taking without the added assumption.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 97

questions.stem: Why can persistent profits attract entry in a competitive model?

options.text: Profits guarantee that market price will remain unchanged
New firms remove all customer demand
Entry is prohibited whenever profits rise
New firms seek profitable opportunities, increasing competitive pressure

questions.explanation: Free entry helps explain the long-run erosion of economic profit; short-run profits remain possible.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slides 5, 8

questions.stem: Which description best fits monopoly in the deck?

options.text: Many small differentiated sellers with free entry
Many suppliers selling identical products with no barriers
One supplier with substantial entry barriers and no close substitute for its product
Few firms whose choices always have no effect on rivals

questions.explanation: The monopoly characteristics contrast with competitive and oligopolistic structures.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slide 11

questions.stem: Why is a monopolist not free to sell unlimited output at any chosen price?

options.text: A monopoly has no customers
A monopoly always receives a legally fixed price
The demand relationship still constrains what buyers will purchase
Its marginal revenue is necessarily identical to price

questions.explanation: Market power means influence over price, not independence from demand.
questions.source: EC2204 Market Structure deck (39 slides); slide-grounded coverage; slides 11, 16–17

questions.stem: A water network has high fixed costs and low marginal costs, making one supplier cheaper than duplicated networks. Which concept describes this?

options.text: Product differentiation
Natural monopoly
Monopolistic competition
Oligopolistic interdependence

questions.stem: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q and marginal cost MC = 20 + 0.5Q. Which output–price pair maximises profit?
questions.explanation: TR = (100 − 2Q)Q, so MR = 100 − 4Q. Equating MR with MC gives 100 − 4Q = 20 + 0.5Q, hence Q = 80/4.5 ≈ 17.78. Price is read from demand: P = 100 − 2(17.78) ≈ €64.44. Rounded, this is Q ≈ 18 and P ≈ €64.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q16; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

questions.stem: Two supermarket chains repeatedly compete in a small town. Each has an incentive to discount if the rival maintains its price, but both would earn more if neither discounted. Which explanation is strongest?

options.text: Monopolistic competition: strategic interaction is impossible.
Natural monopoly: one firm must have falling average cost at every output.
Perfect competition: each chain is necessarily a price taker.
An oligopoly prisoner’s dilemma: individually attractive discounting can leave both worse off.

questions.explanation: The two chains are strategically interdependent. Each has an individual incentive to discount, although mutual restraint would make both better off. This is the incentive conflict in an oligopoly prisoner’s dilemma.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q17; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

questions.stem: A patented pharmaceutical product faces an approaching patent expiry, powerful hospital purchasing groups and a high-cost regulatory approval process for new entrants. Which combination best describes Porter’s forces?

options.text: Patent expiry permanently eliminates rivalry.
Buyer power is high; threat of entry is constrained by regulation, while the patent expiry may intensify rivalry or substitutes.
Threat of entry is automatically high because regulation is costly.
Buyer power is necessarily low because hospitals are large.

questions.explanation: Powerful purchasing groups indicate high buyer power. Costly regulatory approval constrains entry. Patent expiry can expose the product to stronger competition, especially generic entry and subsequent rivalry; it does not eliminate rivalry. The precise substitute classification depends on the industry boundary.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q18; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.

chapters.title: Tutorial 1 — Butter Market & Supply Adjustment
chapters.description: Application of demand, supply, stocks versus flows, and short- versus long-run supply responsiveness to the historical butter-market handout.

questions.stem: In the tutorial’s 2014 European butter market, Russia bans imports of EU food. Holding other determinants constant, what is the immediate demand-and-supply interpretation?

options.text: Demand shifts right because Russian consumers can no longer legally import it.
The existing demand curve shifts only because the butter price falls.
Demand for European butter shifts left, lowering equilibrium price and quantity.
European butter supply shifts right because the ban raises farm productivity.

questions.explanation: The embargo removes an export outlet. This reduces demand facing EU producers; the price fall is an outcome, not the reason the demand curve shifts.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: The butter case reports greater consumer preference for ingredients perceived as natural. How should this be represented in the butter market, other things equal?

options.text: A downward movement along an unchanged demand curve caused by a lower butter price.
A leftward shift of supply caused directly by a change in production technology.
A rightward shift of supply because preferences are a production input.
A rightward shift of the demand curve.

questions.explanation: Changing tastes are a demand determinant: more butter is wanted at a given price. The case’s perception claim is not a dietary recommendation.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: The tutorial describes European dairy farmers leaving production after earlier low prices. Holding demand constant, what is the later supply effect?

options.text: Supply shifts left as less productive capacity remains in the market.
Demand shifts left because every farmer is a butter consumer.
Supply shifts right because fewer firms necessarily supply more.
Only a movement down the original demand curve occurs, with no supply change.

questions.explanation: Exit reduces the quantity producers can offer at given prices. It is a supply change rather than simply a new price along unchanged supply.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: For the tutorial’s 2017 butter market, demand shifts right while supply shifts left. With standard downward demand and upward supply, which outcome is unambiguous?

options.text: Equilibrium quantity is unchanged regardless of the size of either shift.
Equilibrium price rises; the change in equilibrium quantity depends on the relative shifts.
Both equilibrium price and quantity must rise.
Both equilibrium price and quantity must fall.

questions.explanation: Both shifts push price upwards but have opposing quantity effects. Quantity cannot be determined without more information.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: Butter demand rises suddenly, but herds and production facilities take time to expand. What does this imply about price elasticity of supply?

options.text: Long-run supply must be less elastic because more adjustments are possible.
The time horizon affects demand only, not supply.
Supply is generally less elastic in the short run than when producers have time to adjust capacity.
Supply must be perfectly elastic immediately because butter can be sold.

questions.explanation: Capacity and biological production constraints limit immediate output responses. More adjustment options normally become available over a longer period.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: Why can available butter inventories help suppliers respond to an unexpected demand increase?

options.text: Inventories shift consumers’ tastes away from butter automatically.
Selling stocks increases the size of dairy herds immediately.
Stocks guarantee that demand changes can never affect prices.
Stocks can be released before additional current production is available.

questions.explanation: Inventories offer a temporary source of market supply; they do not create unlimited production capacity.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: The tutorial reports a much larger percentage fall in butter stockpiles than in annual production. Why should these figures not be treated as the same measure?

options.text: Stocks measure an amount held at a point in time, while production measures output over a period.
Production and stocks are alternative names for annual consumption.
A percentage change in stocks is always equal to a percentage change in production.
Stockpiles can change only if production stops completely.

questions.explanation: Stocks and flows differ. Sales can draw down accumulated inventories even when production falls much less proportionately.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: Wholesale butter prices and retail butter prices rise by different percentages in the case. What is the soundest inference?

options.text: The figures alone establish the price elasticity of demand.
Price changes need not pass through to different stages of the supply chain in identical proportions.
The two figures contradict each other because all stages must use the same percentage price change.
The figures prove that retailers sell butter at a loss.

questions.explanation: Wholesale and retail prices describe different transaction stages. Their changes alone do not establish margins, losses or an elasticity.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: Russia accounted for a stated share of EU butter exports before its embargo. What denominator must be retained when interpreting that share?

options.text: World butter production, because all exports are global.
All domestic EU butter sales, excluding exports.
EU butter exports, not all EU butter sales or production.
All EU household expenditure.

questions.explanation: An export-market share does not describe the same proportion of all output or sales; changing the denominator misstates the case.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

questions.stem: A student says, “The higher 2017 butter price caused demand to shift right.” Which correction is best?

options.text: An increase in a good’s own price always shifts its demand curve right.
The price increase proves that supply shifted right.
A demand curve cannot be used when exports exist.
Higher demand from tastes and export markets shifted demand; the resulting price increase is not itself a demand shifter.

questions.explanation: Distinguish an own-price movement along a demand curve from shifts caused by non-price determinants, such as preferences or foreign demand.
questions.source: EC2204 Tutorial 1, 22 October 2026; “Europe is running out of butter”, CNNMoney (London), 9 August 2017 (abridged), original tutorial handout.

chapters.title: Absolute & Comparative Advantage, PPFs & Trade
chapters.description: Week 7 Lecture #13: opportunity cost, comparative advantage, PPFs, specialisation and terms of trade; with the OpenStax §33.3 extension on intra-industry trade, economies of scale, variety and dynamic comparative advantage.

questions.stem: A country can produce more of both goods than its trading partner. What determines which good it should specialise in under the comparative-advantage framework?

options.text: Which good has the higher maximum output in the country with greater productivity.
Which good each country can produce at the lower opportunity cost.
Which good has the higher domestic price before trade.
Which country has the higher output in every activity.

questions.explanation: Comparative advantage is determined by relative opportunity costs, not by absolute output alone. A country can have absolute advantage in both goods while each country still has a comparative advantage in one.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 2–3 and 6–9

questions.stem: Ireland can produce at most 16 software units or 40 food units, while Portugal can produce at most 8 software units or 32 food units. Which country has comparative advantage in software?

options.text: Ireland, because its opportunity cost is 2.5 food units per software unit, below Portugal’s 4.
Portugal, because its maximum software output is lower.
Both countries, because Ireland has absolute advantage in software.
Neither country, because their maximum food outputs differ.

questions.explanation: Ireland’s opportunity cost of one software unit is 40 ÷ 16 = 2.5 food units. Portugal’s is 32 ÷ 8 = 4 food units, so Ireland gives up less food when producing software.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 6–9

questions.stem: Using the same production limits—Ireland: 16 software or 40 food; Portugal: 8 software or 32 food—which country has comparative advantage in food?

options.text: Ireland, because it can produce more food in total.
Ireland, because its opportunity cost of food is 0.4 software per food unit.
Portugal, because its opportunity cost of food is 0.25 software per food unit, below Ireland’s 0.4.
Neither, because the two opportunity costs must be equal.

questions.explanation: Portugal gives up 8 ÷ 32 = 0.25 software units to produce one food unit, compared with Ireland’s 16 ÷ 40 = 0.4. The lower opportunity cost gives Portugal comparative advantage in food.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 8–9

questions.stem: On a production possibilities frontier with software on the horizontal axis and food on the vertical axis, what does the magnitude of the slope represent?

options.text: The number of software units gained from one extra unit of food.
Total output from producing both goods at once.
The market price of software relative to food.
The food units forgone for one additional software unit, given the stated resources and technology.

questions.explanation: With software on the horizontal axis and food on the vertical axis, the magnitude of the PPF slope measures food sacrificed per additional software unit—the opportunity cost of software.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 4–5

questions.stem: What assumption about opportunity cost is represented by a straight-line production possibilities frontier?

options.text: Opportunity cost remains constant as production moves along the frontier.
Opportunity cost falls to zero at every point on the frontier.
Both goods can be produced without trade-offs.
Technology and resources increase whenever output changes.

questions.explanation: A straight-line PPF assumes constant opportunity cost: the amount of the other good sacrificed for an additional unit does not change along the line.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF p. 5

questions.stem: Ireland gives up 2.5 food units to produce one software unit, while Portugal gives up 4. If five software units are exchanged for 18 food units, why can this terms-of-trade rate benefit both countries?

options.text: The rate is below both opportunity costs, so both countries produce more food.
The rate is 3.6 food per software—between 2.5 and 4—so each can trade at a rate better than its own production trade-off.
The rate equals Ireland’s opportunity cost, so Portugal necessarily gains more.
The rate is above both opportunity costs, so both countries must lose.

questions.explanation: Eighteen food divided by five software is 3.6 food per software. Because 3.6 lies between Ireland’s 2.5 and Portugal’s 4, Ireland receives more food per software than it would obtain through its own trade-off, while Portugal gives up less food per software than its own production cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF p. 12

questions.stem: In a trade illustration, Ireland moves from a self-sufficiency bundle of (10 software, 15 food) to (11, 18), while Portugal moves from (5 software, 12 food) to (5, 14). What conclusion follows from these stated bundles?

options.text: Only Ireland benefits, because Portugal’s software consumption is unchanged.
Neither benefits, because Portugal does not increase both goods.
Both can be better off: Ireland consumes more of both goods and Portugal keeps the same software while consuming more food.
The bundles prove that both countries produced both goods after specialising.

questions.explanation: Compared with their stated self-sufficiency bundles, Ireland gains one software and three food units. Portugal keeps software consumption unchanged and gains two food units, so neither bundle is worse and each improves in at least one good.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 10–11

questions.stem: After specialisation and trade, Ireland consumes 11 software units and 18 food units; producing 11 software units domestically would leave capacity for only 12.5 food units. How is the post-trade bundle possible?

options.text: Trade separates consumption from domestic production, allowing the country to consume beyond its own PPF.
The PPF measures imports, so the bundle is still domestic production.
Comparative advantage removes the resource constraint from the PPF.
The example assumes Ireland’s technology changes after the exchange.

questions.explanation: The PPF limits what Ireland can produce with its own resources and technology. Specialisation and exchange allow it to consume a bundle that lies beyond that domestic production frontier.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 10–11

questions.stem: A simplified model says GenAI can produce 20 drafts or 4 judgement cases per hour, while a human can produce 5 drafts or 2 judgement cases. Which producer has comparative advantage in judgement cases?

options.text: GenAI, because it has the higher maximum output in both tasks.
GenAI, because it gives up 5 drafts per judgement case, more than the human.
Neither, because the human has lower absolute output.
The human, because one judgement case costs 2.5 drafts for the human but 5 drafts for GenAI.

questions.explanation: The human’s opportunity cost of one judgement case is 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 drafts. GenAI’s is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 drafts, so the human has the lower opportunity cost in judgement cases even though GenAI has absolute advantage in both tasks.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 14–16

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of using the lecture’s simplified GenAI–human comparative-advantage example to predict employment outcomes?

options.text: Comparative advantage cannot apply to tasks performed by people and technology.
The model shows potential gains from specialisation, but employment and who gains also depend on factors such as wages, costs, quality, demand and institutions.
Absolute advantage guarantees that GenAI replaces every human task.
The model proves that specialisation creates equal gains for every worker.

questions.explanation: The slides explicitly treat the example as simplified. Comparative advantage can identify potential gains from specialisation, but it does not guarantee job security or equal gains; real outcomes also depend on wages, AI costs, quality, demand, task redesign and institutions.
questions.source: EC2204 Week 7 Lecture #13, PDF pp. 17–19

questions.stem: What is intra-industry trade?

options.text: A country exports every product it makes and imports no goods from the same industries.
Trade that occurs only between countries with very different opportunity costs.
A country both imports and exports goods from the same industry.
Trade in intermediate goods that never cross a national border.

questions.explanation: Intra-industry trade is trade in goods within the same industry between countries; a country may both export and import goods from that industry.
questions.source: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, §33.3, “The Prevalence of Intra-Industry Trade between Similar Economies”

questions.stem: How can splitting a product’s value chain across firms or countries create gains from intra-industry trade?

options.text: It lets firms specialise in particular stages or products, supporting learning and distinctive skills.
It ensures every country produces the complete finished product independently.
It eliminates the need to exchange components or information.
It makes workers’ skills identical across all firms.

questions.explanation: A value chain is the sequence of stages involved in producing a good. Dividing stages among specialised firms and locations can support learning, innovation and product-specific skills.
questions.source: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, §33.3, “Gains from Specialization and Learning”

questions.stem: An OpenStax example shows average cost falling from $30 at 30 toaster ovens to $10 at 150, then remaining $10 at 200. What does the example illustrate?

options.text: Average cost must fall every time output rises, without limit.
The firm has constant average cost at all production levels.
The largest plant necessarily has a higher average cost than the smallest.
Economies of scale reduce average cost up to a point; beyond that point, added scale need not reduce it further.

questions.explanation: The example shows average cost declining as production rises through 150 units, then staying at $10 at 200 units. Economies of scale operate up to a point, not necessarily indefinitely.
questions.source: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, §33.3, Figure 33.5

questions.stem: Why can international trade allow consumers to benefit from large-scale production without losing all product choice?

options.text: Trade prevents firms from growing large enough to lower average costs.
Large producers in different countries can sell into wider markets, while competition among them can preserve variety and encourage responsiveness.
Economies of scale remove competition, so variety is guaranteed by a single producer.
Consumers must choose only between domestically produced varieties.

questions.explanation: OpenStax explains that international trade can combine the lower average costs of large-scale production with competition and variety because producers in different countries can serve wider markets.
questions.source: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, §33.3, “Economies of Scale, Competition, Variety”

questions.stem: What does dynamic comparative advantage mean in the context of intra-industry trade?

options.text: A country’s comparative advantage is permanently fixed by its climate and geography.
Comparative advantage disappears whenever firms trade within the same industry.
Comparative advantage can change over time as learning, specialised skills and value-chain organisation evolve.
Only a country’s absolute output can change over time.

questions.explanation: The section broadens the comparative-advantage framework: specialised learning, new skills and changes in value chains can alter relative productivity and comparative advantage over time.
questions.source: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, §33.3, “Dynamic Comparative Advantage”

questions.stem: With fixed resources and technology, how should production points inside, on and outside a production possibilities frontier be classified, respectively?

options.text: Efficient; inefficient; attainable
Unattainable; efficient; inefficient
Inefficient; productively efficient; currently unattainable through domestic production
Inefficient; unattainable; productively efficient

questions.explanation: Inside points leave productive capacity inefficiently used; frontier points use it efficiently; outside points exceed domestic production possibilities under the stated resources and technology.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #14, 27 October 2026 — notes and transcript, PPFs and comparative advantage; current Ireland–Portugal example where relevant. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c819887b8ec88f26ba98d ; Materials: https://app.notion.com/p/0ad4b0a285f8455bbc94426d4dc12643

questions.stem: Portugal specialises completely in food while Ireland shifts towards software but continues producing some food. Must Ireland also specialise completely for both countries to gain from trade?

options.text: Yes; both countries must produce only one good
No; shifting production towards comparative advantage can allow gains without both specialising completely
Yes; partial specialisation eliminates opportunity cost
No; gains arise only if the countries have identical opportunity costs

questions.explanation: The delivered example has Portugal fully specialising and Ireland producing both goods. Reallocation towards lower-opportunity-cost activities and suitable exchange can still benefit both.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #14, 27 October 2026 — notes and transcript, PPFs and comparative advantage; current Ireland–Portugal example where relevant. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c819887b8ec88f26ba98d ; Materials: https://app.notion.com/p/0ad4b0a285f8455bbc94426d4dc12643

questions.stem: A student claims that exchanging goods creates extra physical output even if neither country changes production. Which statement best distinguishes exchange from production gains?

options.text: Exchange automatically creates additional goods
Exchange shifts both domestic PPFs outward
Production is irrelevant once trade starts
Reallocating production can raise combined output; exchange distributes the available goods between the parties

questions.explanation: Trade does not create goods merely by exchanging them. In the lecture, production reallocation increases combined output and exchange lets both countries share the gains.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #14, 27 October 2026 — notes and transcript, PPFs and comparative advantage; current Ireland–Portugal example where relevant. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c819887b8ec88f26ba98d ; Materials: https://app.notion.com/p/0ad4b0a285f8455bbc94426d4dc12643

questions.stem: With equal labour resources and straight-line PPFs, Ireland can produce 32 software or 80 food; Portugal can produce 16 software or 64 food. What are their opportunity costs of one food unit, respectively?

options.text: 2.5 software and 4 software
0.4 software and 0.25 software
0.25 software and 0.4 software
32 software and 16 software

questions.explanation: Food opportunity cost is maximum software divided by maximum food: Ireland 32/80=0.4 software per food; Portugal 16/64=0.25. Keep the units attached to the ratio. Optional understanding practice: the lecture notes prioritise definitions, not maths, for this topic.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #14, 27 October 2026 — notes and transcript, PPFs and comparative advantage; current Ireland–Portugal example where relevant. https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c819887b8ec88f26ba98d ; Materials: https://app.notion.com/p/0ad4b0a285f8455bbc94426d4dc12643

questions.stem: Ireland’s straight-line PPF has endpoints of 32 software and 80 food. If it produces 28 software efficiently, how much food can it also produce?

options.text: 10 food
52 food
70 food
80 food

questions.explanation: One software costs 80/32=2.5 food. At 28 software, food production is 80−2.5×28=10. Optional understanding practice: the lecture notes prioritise definitions, not maths, for this topic.

questions.stem: Ireland produces (28 software,10 food) and Portugal produces (0 software,64 food). Ireland sends 10 software to Portugal in exchange for 31 food. Which pair of post-trade consumption bundles is correct?

options.text: Ireland (18,31); Portugal (10,33)
Ireland (38,41); Portugal (10,33)
Ireland (18,41); Portugal (10,33)
Ireland (18,41); Portugal (10,95)

questions.explanation: Ireland retains 28−10=18 software and has 10+31=41 food. Portugal receives 10 software and retains 64−31=33 food. Total consumption equals total production. Optional understanding practice: the lecture notes prioritise definitions, not maths, for this topic.

questions.stem: Before specialisation, Ireland produces (16 software,40 food) and Portugal (8 software,32 food). Afterwards, Ireland produces (28 software,10 food) and Portugal (0 software,64 food). How does combined output change?

options.text: +12 software and −30 food
+4 software and +4 food
+28 software and +74 food
+4 software and +2 food

questions.explanation: Initial totals are (24 software,72 food); new totals are (28,74). Combined output increases by four software and two food. Optional understanding practice: the lecture notes prioritise definitions, not maths, for this topic.

questions.stem: Ireland can produce food domestically at an opportunity cost of 2.5 food per software unit exported. Portugal offers only 2.4 food for each software unit. For an exchange of 10 software, how much less food would Ireland receive than it could produce by reallocating the equivalent resources domestically?

options.text: 1 food unit
0.1 food unit
24 food units
25 food units

questions.explanation: Exporting ten software forgoes the resources to produce 25 food domestically. The offer provides 24 food, one less than that alternative. The offered rate is below Ireland’s opportunity cost. Optional understanding practice: the lecture notes prioritise definitions, not maths, for this topic.

questions.stem: Ireland’s straight-line PPF has endpoints of 32 software or 80 food. What is its maximum domestic food production at 18 software, compared with consumption of 41 food after trade?

options.text: 45 food domestically; 41 is inside its frontier
62 food domestically; 41 is inside its frontier
35 food domestically; 41 is beyond its domestic production frontier at that software quantity
41 food domestically; consumption must be on its frontier

questions.explanation: The domestic frontier is F=80−2.5S. At S=18, F=35. Trade can enable consumption of 41 food at the same software quantity without enabling that combination as domestic production. Optional understanding practice: the lecture notes prioritise definitions, not maths, for this topic.

questions.stem: With equal resources, the US can produce 500 planes or 1,000 tons of shoes; China can produce 100 planes or 800 tons of shoes. Assuming straight-line PPFs, what are their opportunity costs of one plane and which has comparative advantage in planes?

options.text: US 0.5 tons; China 0.125 tons; China
US 2 tons; China 8 tons; China
US 8 tons; China 2 tons; US
US 2 tons; China 8 tons; US

questions.explanation: US cost=1,000/500=2 tons per plane; China cost=800/100=8. The US sacrifices fewer shoes per plane and therefore has comparative advantage in planes. Optional understanding practice: the lecture notes prioritise definitions, not maths, for this topic.

questions.stem: A human analyst can complete 6 routine reconciliations or 3 client reviews per day; an AI system can complete 30 reconciliations or 5 reviews per day. Assume comparable output and one day each. Which allocation follows comparative advantage?

options.text: AI specialises in reviews because 5 exceeds 3.
There can be no gains from specialisation when AI is absolutely better at both.
Human specialises in reconciliations because 6 is fewer than 30.
AI specialises in reconciliations; human in reviews, despite AI’s absolute advantage in both.

questions.explanation: For one reconciliation the human sacrifices 3/6 = 0.5 reviews, while the AI sacrifices 5/30 = 1/6 of a review. The AI therefore has comparative advantage in reconciliations. For one review, the human sacrifices 2 reconciliations versus 6 for the AI, so the human has comparative advantage in reviews despite the AI’s absolute advantage in both tasks.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q20; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.
